core: While India has designated 18 domestic Biosphere Reserves under its National Biosphere Reserve Programme, only a subset is internationally recognized under UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR). Reserves such as Manas, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dihang-Dibang, Kachchh, and Seshachalam Hills remain domestic Biosphere Reserves outside the UNESCO WNBR.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve (encompassing Campbell Bay and Galathea National Parks) was inducted into UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR) in 2013, and the Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve (straddling Kerala and Tamil Nadu in the Southern Western Ghats) was inducted into the WNBR in 2016.

Statement 2 is correct. Khangchendzonga Biosphere Reserve (Sikkim), covering sub-tropical to alpine ecosystems in the Eastern Himalayas, was included in UNESCO's WNBR in 2018, and Panna Biosphere Reserve (Madhya Pradesh), a critical tiger and vulture habitat drained by the Ken River, was included in UNESCO's WNBR in 2020.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Not all domestically notified Biosphere Reserves in North-East India are part of UNESCO's WNBR. While Nokrek (Meghalaya) and Khangchendzonga (Sikkim) are part of UNESCO's WNBR, Manas (Assam), Dibru-Saikhowa (Assam), and Dihang-Dibang (Arunachal Pradesh) are domestically designated Biosphere Reserves under the MoEFCC programme and are not included in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves (note that while Manas is a UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site, it is not in the MAB World Network of Biosphere Reserves).

ref: UNESCO MAB World Network of Biosphere Reserves Directory; MoEFCC Annual Report

stem: With reference to the legal framework governing Tiger Reserves in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A Tiger Reserve comprises both a core or critical tiger habitat required to be kept inviolate for tiger conservation and a peripheral buffer area aimed at promoting coexistence between wildlife and human activity.

2. The formal notification declaring an area as a Tiger Reserve in the Official Gazette is issued directly by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) in consultation with the concerned State Wildlife Board.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Section 38V(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the legal power to notify an area as a Tiger Reserve vests in the State Government, which acts upon the recommendation of the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA). Every Tiger Reserve is statutorily structured into an inviolate core/critical tiger habitat and a multi-use peripheral buffer zone.

exp.why: Under Section 38V(4) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, a Tiger Reserve includes two distinct zones: (i) a core or critical tiger habitat (areas of National Parks and Sanctuaries required to be kept inviolate for tiger conservation without affecting the rights of Scheduled Tribes or other forest dwellers), and (ii) a buffer or peripheral area with a lesser degree of habitat protection to ensure the integrity of the critical habitat while promoting coexistence between wildlife and human activity.

Neither the Central Government nor the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) directly issues the gazette notification constituting a Tiger Reserve. Under Section 38V(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, it is the State Government that notifies an area as a Tiger Reserve on the recommendation of the NTCA.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Section 38V(1) and Section 38V(4).

stem: With reference to the distinction between 'Critical Tiger Habitat' (CTH) and 'Critical Wildlife Habitat' (CWH) in Indian environmental law, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While Critical Tiger Habitats are statutorily defined under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Critical Wildlife Habitats are defined under the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006.

2. Both Critical Tiger Habitats and Critical Wildlife Habitats can be notified across any Reserved Forest, Protected Forest, or Community Reserve located outside National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.

3. Once a Critical Wildlife Habitat from which forest rights holders have been relocated is notified, the area cannot subsequently be diverted by the State Government, the Central Government, or any other entity for other uses.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Critical Tiger Habitats (CTH) are governed by Section 38V(4)(i) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 specifically for the core areas of Tiger Reserves, whereas Critical Wildlife Habitats (CWH) are defined under Section 2(b) and Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 for National Parks and Sanctuaries generally. Both categories are legally restricted to areas within National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries, and relocated CWH areas carry an absolute statutory bar against subsequent diversion for any other use.

exp.why: The Explanation to Section 38V(4)(i) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (inserted via the 2006 Amendment) defines 'core or critical tiger habitat', whereas 'critical wildlife habitat' (CWH) is statutorily defined solely under Section 2(b) of the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA).

Neither CTH nor CWH can be notified in general Reserved Forests, Protected Forests, or Community Reserves located outside National Parks and Sanctuaries. Section 38V(4)(i) of the WPA, 1972 defines CTH as 'areas of National Parks and sanctuaries' kept inviolate for tiger conservation, and Section 2(b) of the FRA, 2006 similarly defines CWH as 'such areas of National Parks and Sanctuaries' established on scientific criteria as required to be kept inviolate for wildlife conservation.

Under the second proviso to Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006, once a Critical Wildlife Habitat from which forest rights holders have been relocated for wildlife conservation is notified, that land cannot subsequently be diverted by the State Government, the Central Government, or any other entity for any other uses.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Section 38V(4)(i); Forest Rights Act, 2006, Section 2(b) and Section 4(2).

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the governance and statutory protection of Tiger Reserves in India:
items: Statement-I: Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, no State Government can alter the boundaries of a Tiger Reserve or de-notify it except on the recommendation of the National Tiger Conservation Authority and with the approval of the National Board for Wildlife.

Statement-II: The Union Minister in charge of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Tiger Conservation Authority, whereas the Prime Minister serves as the ex-officio Chairperson of the National Board for Wildlife.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Section 38W of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 creates a dual statutory lock requiring both the recommendation/approval of the NTCA and the approval of the NBWL before any State Government can alter the boundaries of or de-notify a Tiger Reserve. While the Environment Minister chairs the NTCA and the Prime Minister chairs the NBWL, this institutional chairing structure does not explain the statutory safeguard in Section 38W.

exp.why: Under Section 38W(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, no alteration in the boundaries of a Tiger Reserve can be made except on a recommendation of the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) and the approval of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL). Similarly, Section 38W(2) mandates that no State Government shall de-notify a Tiger Reserve except in public interest with the approval of both the NTCA and the NBWL.

Under Section 38L(2)(a) of the WPA, 1972, the Minister in charge of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change is the Chairperson of the NTCA, while under Section 5A(1)(a), the Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the NBWL. Although factually correct, this difference in ex-officio leadership does not explain why Section 38W imposes a dual-clearance lock on boundary alteration and de-notification (which exists to prevent unilateral state-level dilution of critical tiger habitats and corridors).

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Sections 5A, 38L, and 38W.

stem: With reference to the Tiger Conservation Plan (TCP) and the Tiger Conservation Foundation under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The State Government is statutorily required to establish a Tiger Conservation Foundation for Tiger Reserves within the State, which is empowered to recycle entry fees and eco-tourism receipts collected in the reserve to foster stakeholder development.
2. All gate receipts and tourism fees collected by a Tiger Conservation Foundation must first be credited to the Consolidated Fund of India and subsequently disbursed through the National CAMPA Fund.
3. The statutory Tiger Conservation Plan for each Tiger Reserve is drafted directly by the Wildlife Institute of India and requires formal ratification by Parliament before coming into force.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Section 38X of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, State Governments establish Tiger Conservation Foundations to retain and directly recycle gate fees and tourism revenue at the reserve level for conservation and local eco-development without routing them through the Consolidated Fund or CAMPA. Under Section 38V(3) and Section 38O(1)(a), the Tiger Conservation Plan is prepared by the State Government and approved by the NTCA.

exp.why: Under Section 38X(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the State Government shall establish a Tiger Conservation Foundation for Tiger Reserves within the State to facilitate ecological, economic, social, and cultural development. Under Section 38X(2)(e), one of its explicit statutory objectives is to augment and mobilize financial resources, including the recycling of entry and other fees received in a Tiger Reserve, to foster stakeholder development and eco-tourism.

The core legislative purpose behind creating Tiger Conservation Foundations (typically registered as trusts or societies under Section 38X) is to allow revenue generated from entry fees, tourism charges, and donations to be retained and ploughed back directly into the management of the Tiger Reserve and local community eco-development, bypassing treasury delays in the Consolidated Fund and separate from the CAMPA mechanism.

Under Section 38V(3) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the Tiger Conservation Plan (TCP) for each reserve is prepared by the concerned State Government (not drafted directly by the Wildlife Institute of India), and under Section 38O(1)(a), it is evaluated and approved by the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), without any requirement of parliamentary ratification.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Sections 38O(1)(a), 38V(3), and 38X.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the legal status of Elephant Reserves and Elephant Corridors in India:
items: Statement-I: Like Tiger Reserves under Chapter IV-B of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Elephant Reserves and Elephant Corridors constitute a distinct standalone statutory category of Protected Areas under the Act, automatically prohibiting all mining and linear infrastructure upon notification.

Statement-II: Elephant Reserves in India are notified administratively by State Governments under Project Elephant across mosaic landscapes encompassing Protected Areas, Reserved Forests, and revenue lands, deriving statutory protection only to the extent that their constituent pockets are notified under wildlife, forest, or environmental statutes.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike Tiger Reserves, which enjoy dedicated statutory backing under Chapter IV-B of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, neither Elephant Reserves nor Elephant Corridors are a standalone statutory category of Protected Area under the WPA, 1972. They are administrative landscape designations notified by States under Project Elephant, and legal enforcement within them depends on the underlying statutory status of their constituent lands (such as National Parks, Sanctuaries, Community/Conservation Reserves, Reserved Forests, or Eco-Sensitive Zones under the EPA, 1986).

exp.why: Unlike Tiger Reserves (which were accorded statutory status under Chapter IV-B of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 via the 2006 Amendment), 'Elephant Reserves' and 'Elephant Corridors' are not recognized as a standalone statutory category of Protected Areas under the WPA, 1972, nor does an Elephant Reserve notification by itself impose an automatic statutory blanket ban across non-forest revenue lands within its perimeter.

Elephant Reserves are notified through administrative notifications by State Governments (with the approval of the Union Government under Project Elephant) over broader ecological landscapes comprising National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Reserved/Protected Forests, and human-use revenue or private lands. Consequently, statutory enforcement inside an Elephant Reserve or corridor flows from the specific legal regime applicable to each constituent parcel—namely the WPA, 1972 (for Protected Areas), the Indian Forest Act, 1927 / Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 (for forest land), or the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (where notified as an Eco-Sensitive Zone).

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; MoEFCC Project Elephant Guidelines on Elephant Reserves and Corridors.

stem: With reference to the regulatory framework and Supreme Court jurisprudence governing Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) around National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Rather than imposing an absolute prohibition on all human activity, the regulatory regime for Eco-Sensitive Zones functions as a transition shock absorber that classifies activities into prohibited, regulated, and permitted categories, allowing ongoing agriculture by local communities.

2. As per the Supreme Court's modified ruling on Eco-Sensitive Zones, the default requirement of maintaining a minimum 1-kilometre ESZ does not apply where the Union Government has issued a site-specific ESZ notification or where the Protected Area is situated along inter-state borders.
3. Eco-Sensitive Zones around National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries are statutorily notified by the respective State Governments under the provisions of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) are notified by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) under Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986—not by State Governments under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Designed as shock absorbers with prohibited, regulated, and permitted tiers, ESZs are governed by site-specific notifications following the Supreme Court's April 2023 modification of its June 2022 uniform 1-km order.

exp.why: Under the MoEFCC's 2011 Guidelines for Declaration of Eco-Sensitive Zones, ESZs act as 'shock absorbers' and transition zones around high-protection areas. Activities are divided into three tiers: Prohibited (e.g., commercial mining, polluting industries, major hydroelectric projects, sawmills), Regulated (e.g., felling of trees, commercial hotels/resorts, widening of roads), and Permitted (e.g., ongoing agricultural and horticultural practices by local communities, rainwater harvesting, organic farming).

In April 2023 (In Re: T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India), the Supreme Court modified its earlier June 2022 blanket directive of a mandatory minimum 1-km ESZ around all Protected Areas. The Court held that the default 1-km rule shall not apply where the MoEFCC has already issued draft or final site-specific ESZ notifications (or finalized pending proposals) or where the National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary is located on inter-state or international borders, while reiterating that mining remains prohibited within 1 km of any National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary.

The term 'Eco-Sensitive Zone' is not created under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, nor is it notified by State Governments. ESZs are notified by the Central Government (Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change) in exercise of powers conferred by Section 3(2)(v) of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 read with Rule 5 of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986.

ref: Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, Section 3(2)(v); Supreme Court Judgment in T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (April 2023).

stem: With reference to the regulatory framework governing Eco-Sensitive Zones (ESZs) notified around Protected Areas under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Setting up of new sawmills, commercial use of firewood, and establishment of new major hydroelectric projects are categorized as prohibited activities within an Eco-Sensitive Zone.
2. Ongoing agricultural and horticultural practices by local communities, along with organic farming and rainwater harvesting, are categorized as permitted activities.
3. The establishment of new hotels and resorts and the felling of trees on private revenue land are classified as prohibited activities within an Eco-Sensitive Zone.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: MoEFCC guidelines classify human activities inside Eco-Sensitive Zones into three tiers—Prohibited, Regulated, and Permitted—so that ESZs function as transition shock-absorbers rather than exclusionary zones that halt sustainable local livelihoods.

exp.why: Under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) Guidelines for Declaration of Eco-Sensitive Zones around National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries, activities with severe irreversible ecological footprints—including commercial mining, setting up of sawmills, setting up of industries causing pollution, commercial use of firewood, and establishment of new major hydroelectric projects—are strictly prohibited.

Because ESZs are designed as shock-absorber transition zones rather than inviolate cores, benign livelihood activities such as ongoing agriculture and horticulture practices by local communities, rainwater harvesting, organic farming, and adoption of green technology are classified as permitted activities.

Neither the establishment of hotels/resorts nor the felling of trees is completely prohibited in an ESZ; instead, both are classified as regulated activities. Felling of trees on Forest, Government, or private revenue land requires prior permission from the competent authority, and hotels or resorts are regulated in accordance with an approved Zonal Master Plan and eco-tourism guidelines to safeguard wildlife corridors.

ref: MoEFCC Guidelines for Declaration of Eco-Sensitive Zones (2011); Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

stem: With reference to Biodiversity Heritage Sites (BHS) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, a State Government is empowered to notify Biodiversity Heritage Sites in the Official Gazette in consultation with the concerned local bodies, without requiring prior statutory approval from the National Board for Wildlife.
2. Biodiversity Heritage Sites can be notified across terrestrial, inland water, as well as coastal and marine ecosystems that harbor rich wild or domesticated biodiversity.

3. Unlike the declaration of a National Park under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, the notification of a Biodiversity Heritage Site does not automatically extinguish or restrict the prevailing customary practices and usages of local communities, except when the community itself voluntarily decides to regulate them.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Notified by State Governments in consultation with local bodies under Section 37 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, Biodiversity Heritage Sites conserve fragile ecosystems containing wild or domesticated biodiversity without extinguishing community rights.

exp.why: Under Section 37(1) of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, the State Government, in consultation with local bodies (such as Panchayats or Municipalities) and the State Biodiversity Board, may notify areas of biodiversity importance as Biodiversity Heritage Sites in the Official Gazette. The National Board for Wildlife (constituted under the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972) has no statutory approval role in BHS notifications.

As per the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) Guidelines for Selection and Management of Biodiversity Heritage Sites, BHS are well-defined unique and ecologically fragile ecosystems covering terrestrial, coastal, inland water, and marine areas that exhibit high species richness, wild as well as domesticated intra-specific diversity, high endemism, rare and threatened species, or fossil beds.

Unlike National Parks where statutory declaration extinguishes all private and community resource extraction rights, the NBA Guidelines explicitly stipulate that the creation of a BHS does not impose any automatic statutory restriction on the prevailing practices and usages of local communities, other than those voluntarily decided by the communities themselves through the Biodiversity Management Committee (BMC).

ref: Section 37 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002; NBA Guidelines on Biodiversity Heritage Sites

stem: With reference to Sacred Groves serving as traditional community-led in-situ conservation networks across India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Law Kyntang : Meghalaya — Community-protected climax sub-tropical forest patches preserving relic and endemic flora
2. Oran : Himachal Pradesh — High-altitude alpine pastures dedicated to mountain deities
3. Kavu : Maharashtra — Semi-evergreen forest groves along the northern Western Ghats
4. Devrai : Jharkhand — Sal-dominated tribal sacred groves maintained by Chota Nagpur plateau communities
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Sacred groves are age-old community-protected forest patches dedicated to ancestral or folk deities across India—such as Law Kyntang in Meghalaya, Oran in Rajasthan, Kavu in Kerala, Devrai in Maharashtra, and Sarna in Jharkhand—serving as vital refugia for relic and endemic species.

exp.why: Law Kyntang (and Law Lyngdoh) are traditional sacred groves found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya. Maintained under customary tribal governance, they preserve undisturbed climax sub-tropical broadleaf forests, primitive angiosperms, orchids, and endemic medicinal plants.

Orans (along with Jogmaya and Kankad Bani) are traditional sacred groves and community pasturelands of arid and semi-arid Rajasthan, where cutting of trees like Khejri (Prosopis cineraria) is prohibited by community custom, providing crucial habitat for the Great Indian Bustard and Chinkara. In Himachal Pradesh, sacred groves are locally known as Dev Van.

Kavu (and Sarpakavu) are the traditional sacred groves of Kerala along the Malabar coast and southern Western Ghats, acting as important refugia for rare Myristica swamp flora, lianas, and amphibians. Sacred groves in Maharashtra are called Devrai or Deorai.

Devrai (or Deorai) is the regional name for sacred groves in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra and Goa. The Sal-dominated (Shorea robusta) sacred groves maintained by tribal communities of the Chota Nagpur plateau in Jharkhand, Bihar, and Odisha are known as Sarna or Jaherthan.

ref: ENVIS Centre on Conservation of Ecological Heritage and Sacred Sites of India; NCERT Class XII Biology

stem: Consider the following pairs of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) in India and their characteristic ecological and geographical features:
items: 1. Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park : Extensive seagrass meadows supporting Dugongs and fringing coral reefs across 21 islands off the Tamil Nadu coast
2. Gahirmatha Marine Wildlife Sanctuary : Largest mass nesting (arribada) beach of Leatherback sea turtles located along the Andhra Pradesh coast
3. Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park (Wandoor) : Atoll coral reef formation located in the Lakshadweep archipelago
4. Malvan Marine Wildlife Sanctuary : Intertidal mudflats and coral reefs situated in the Gulf of Kutch, Gujarat
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India's network of Marine Protected Areas spans specialized coastal and island ecosystems—including the seagrass and fringing reefs of the Gulf of Mannar (Tamil Nadu), the Olive Ridley rookeries of Gahirmatha (Odisha), the patch reefs of Malvan (Maharashtra), and the island reefs of Wandoor (Andaman).

exp.why: The Gulf of Mannar Marine National Park encompasses 21 islets and adjacent shallow coastal waters between Rameswaram and Thoothukudi in Tamil Nadu. It forms the core of the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve and harbors rich seagrass beds (critical foraging habitat for the vulnerable Dugong), mangroves, and fringing and patch coral reefs.

Gahirmatha Marine Wildlife Sanctuary is located in Odisha (not Andhra Pradesh) along the Bhitarkanika-Dhamra estuarine coast, and it is renowned as the world's largest mass nesting (arribada) rookery for Olive Ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea), not Giant Leatherback turtles (whose primary Indian nesting beaches are in Great Nicobar and Little Andaman Islands).

Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park at Wandoor is located in the South Andaman district of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (comprising the Labyrinth Islands group characterized by fringing coral reefs and mangrove creeks), not in the atoll formations of the Lakshadweep archipelago.

Malvan Marine Wildlife Sanctuary is located in the Sindhudurg district along the Konkan coast of Maharashtra (featuring rocky intertidal shores, Sindhudurg Fort, and patch corals). The Marine National Park and Sanctuary located in the Gulf of Kutch (Jamnagar/Devbhumi Dwarka) is a separate MPA in Gujarat.

ref: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) ENVIS Database on Marine Protected Areas of India

stem: With reference to transboundary conservation landscapes and contiguous Protected Areas along India's international borders, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Manas National Park in Assam shares a contiguous international ecological boundary with the Royal Manas National Park in Bhutan, forming a unified transboundary habitat for tigers, Asian elephants, and golden langurs.

2. Within the Terai Arc Landscape, Valmiki Tiger Reserve in Bihar forms a direct contiguous transboundary forest block with Bardiya National Park in western Nepal, whereas Katarniaghat Wildlife Sanctuary in Uttar Pradesh adjoins Chitwan National Park in eastern Nepal.

3. The Indian Sundarbans National Park and the Bangladesh Sundarbans Reserve Forest are separated along their international boundary by the Teesta and Barak rivers, which act as the freshwater barrier between the two mangrove sectors.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Transboundary ecological corridors connect Indian Protected Areas with contiguous habitats in neighboring countries—such as Manas (Assam) with Royal Manas (Bhutan), Valmiki (Bihar) with Chitwan (Nepal), Katarniaghat/Dudhwa (UP) with Bardiya/Shuklaphanta (Nepal), and the Indo-Bangladesh Sundarbans across the Raimangal river system.

exp.why: Manas National Park and Tiger Reserve in Assam lies directly contiguous to Bhutan's Royal Manas National Park across the Himalayan foothills. Together they constitute the Transboundary Manas Conservation Area (TraMCA) drained by the Manas-Beki river system, enabling seasonal movement of tigers, elephants, one-horned rhinoceroses, and golden langurs.

The transboundary pairings within the Terai Arc Landscape are reversed in the statement. Valmiki Tiger Reserve in West Champaran (Bihar) is physically contiguous with Chitwan National Park (and Parsa National Park) in south-central Nepal, whereas Katarniaghat Wildlife Sanctuary (part of Dudhwa Tiger Reserve in Uttar Pradesh) is linked via the Khata biological corridor to Bardiya National Park in western Nepal.

The international boundary separating the Indian Sundarbans (West Bengal) from the Bangladesh Sundarbans Reserve Forest is demarcated by the Ichamati–Kalindi–Raimangal–Hariabhanga estuarine river system, not the Teesta and Barak rivers. The Teesta joins the Brahmaputra (Jamuna) in northern Bangladesh, and the Barak flows through northeast India into the Surma–Kushiyara–Meghna river system.

ref: NTCA Status of Tigers & Co-predators Report; Terai Arc Landscape (TAL) and TraMCA Profiles

stem: Consider the following pairs of National Parks/Tiger Reserves in India and the primary rivers flowing through them:
items: 1. Silent Valley National Park : Kunthipuzha River
2. Namdapha National Park : Noa-Dihing River
3. Panna Tiger Reserve : Chambal River
4. Jim Corbett National Park : Sharda (Mahakali) River
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Perennial river systems act as the ecological lifelines of India's Protected Areas—such as the Kunthipuzha draining Silent Valley, the Noa-Dihing flowing through Namdapha, the Ken bisecting Panna, and the Ramganga meandering through Jim Corbett.

exp.why: The Kunthipuzha River (a major tributary of the Bharathapuzha or Nila River) originates in the Nilgiri highlands and flows north-to-south through the entire length of the undisturbed tropical evergreen rainforests of Silent Valley National Park in Palakkad district, Kerala.

The Noa-Dihing River (a tributary of the Lohit–Brahmaputra river system) originates near the Chaukan Pass on the Indo-Myanmar border and flows east-to-west right through the heart of Namdapha National Park and Tiger Reserve in Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh.

Panna Tiger Reserve in the Vindhyan range of Madhya Pradesh is bisected by the Ken River (a right-bank tributary of the Yamuna), which flows northward for nearly 55 km through the reserve, creating deep gorges and supporting gharials and mugger crocodiles. The Chambal River flows further west through the National Chambal Sanctuary along the Madhya Pradesh–Rajasthan–Uttar Pradesh tri-junction.

Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand is drained primarily by the Ramganga River (along with its tributaries Sonanadi, Mandal, and Palain, and the Kosi River flowing along its eastern boundary), which forms the Kalagarh reservoir inside the reserve. The Sharda (Mahakali) River flows further east along the Indo-Nepal border near Banbasa and Dudhwa/Kishanpur.

ref: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) National Park Profiles; NCERT Class XI India: Physical Environment

stem: With reference to the biogeographic classification of India (developed by Rodgers and Panwar for the Wildlife Institute of India) and its ecological role in planning the national Protected Area network, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: It divides India into ten biogeographic zones and twenty-seven biotic provinces to ensure representative in-situ conservation across major ecosystems, with the Deccan Peninsula accounting for the largest share of the country's geographical area.
opts.B: The Western Ghats biogeographic zone encompasses the second-largest geographical area among the ten zones and consequently accounts for the largest total land area notified under National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries.
opts.C: The Lakshadweep archipelago and the Andaman and Nicobar archipelago are grouped together under the 'Islands' biogeographic zone due to their shared oceanic and coral reef ecology.
opts.D: The Gangetic Plain biogeographic zone has the highest percentage of its own geographical area notified under the Protected Area network owing to extensive alluvial grassland and floodplain sanctuaries.

core: India's Protected Area network is scientifically planned around the Wildlife Institute of India's Biogeographic Classification (10 Biogeographic Zones subdivided into 27 Biotic Provinces) to prevent conservation bias toward a single biome. While the Deccan Peninsula is the largest biogeographic zone (~42% of India's landmass), smaller zones like the Western Ghats and Islands exhibit disproportionately high species endemism.

exp.why: Option (A) is correct because the biogeographic classification by Rodgers, Panwar, and Mathur divides India into 10 Biogeographic Zones (Trans-Himalaya, Himalaya, Desert, Semi-Arid, Western Ghats, Deccan Peninsula, Gangetic Plain, Coasts, North-East, and Islands) and 27 Biotic Provinces to guide representative Protected Area coverage; among these, the Deccan Peninsula is the largest zone, covering approximately 42% of India's landmass. Option (B) is incorrect because the Western Ghats zone covers only about 4% to 5.8% of India's geographical area (making it one of the smaller zones, after Islands, Coasts, and North-East, whereas Semi-Arid, Gangetic Plain, Desert, and Himalaya are much larger). Option (C) is incorrect because in the WII biogeographic classification, the Andaman and Nicobar Islands constitute Zone 10 (Islands: 10A Andaman and 10B Nicobar), whereas the Lakshadweep Islands are classified as a biotic province (8C) within Zone 8 (Coasts). Option (D) is incorrect because the Gangetic Plain has one of the lowest percentages (<2%) of its zone area under Protected Areas due to dense human settlement and intensive agrarian land use.

ref: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) Biogeographic Classification of India (Rodgers, Panwar & Mathur, 2002); MoEFCC National Wildlife Action Plan

stem: With reference to the legal interface between the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) and the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended in 2022) regarding Protected Areas, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The statutory definition of 'forest land' under the Forest Rights Act, 2006 explicitly includes both Wildlife Sanctuaries and National Parks, thereby allowing the recognition of Community Forest Resource (CFR) rights inside Protected Areas.

2. Once an area inside a National Park or Wildlife Sanctuary is notified as a Critical Wildlife Habitat (CWH) under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, it may subsequently be diverted for linear public infrastructure projects only with the prior approval of the National Board for Wildlife.

3. Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, where a Wildlife Sanctuary falls within a Scheduled Area or an area where the Forest Rights Act, 2006 applies, the management plan for the Sanctuary must be prepared after due consultation with the concerned Gram Sabha.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 extends individual and Community Forest Resource (CFR) rights to Sanctuaries and National Parks, while making Critical Wildlife Habitats (CWH) strictly inalienable and non-divertible for any non-forestry use. Furthermore, the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 harmonized Section 33 of the WPA with the FRA by mandating Gram Sabha consultation in preparing Sanctuary management plans.

exp.why: Section 2(d) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006 defines 'forest land' as land of any description falling within any forest area including unclassified forests, undemarcated forests, existing or deemed forests, protected forests, reserved forests, Sanctuaries, and National Parks. Consequently, Gram Sabhas can have their Community Forest Resource (CFR) conservation and management rights recognized under Section 3(1)(i) and Section 5 even within Wildlife Sanctuaries and National Parks.

Under the proviso to Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006, once forest rights are modified or resettled to create an inviolate Critical Wildlife Habitat (CWH) inside a National Park or Sanctuary, 'no such land shall be subsequently diverted by the State Government or the Central Government or any other entity for other uses'. This statutory bar against diversion is absolute and cannot be overridden even by the National Board for Wildlife.

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 amended Section 33 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 by inserting a specific proviso stipulating that if a Sanctuary falls under Scheduled Areas or areas where the Forest Rights Act, 2006 is applicable, the management plan for such Sanctuary shall be prepared after due consultation with the concerned Gram Sabha.

ref: Section 2(d) & Section 4(2) of the Forest Rights Act, 2006; Section 33 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended in 2022)

stem: With reference to the statutory provisions governing Protected Areas and wildlife habitats following the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Every Wildlife Sanctuary must be controlled, managed, and maintained by the Chief Wildlife Warden in accordance with a management plan approved by the Chief Wildlife Warden as per guidelines issued by the Central Government.

2. While granting a new arms licence under the Arms Act, 1959 within ten kilometres of a Wildlife Sanctuary requires the prior concurrence of the Chief Wildlife Warden, the renewal of an existing arms licence for a person residing within that zone cannot be granted except under intimation to the Chief Wildlife Warden or the authorised officer.

3. Under Section 62A of the Act, the statutory definition of 'invasive alien species' encompasses both exotic species introduced from outside India and native Indian species that proliferate invasively outside their natural biogeographic zone within the country.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 strengthened Protected Area governance by mandating CWW-approved management plans for Sanctuaries (Section 33) and requiring mandatory intimation to the Chief Wildlife Warden or authorised officer before renewing existing arms licences within 10 km of a PA (Section 34(4), supplementing the prior concurrence required for new licences under Section 34(3)). However, Section 2(16A) restricts the statutory definition of 'invasive alien species' strictly to species that are 'not native to India'.

exp.why: The 2022 Amendment amended Section 33(a) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 to mandate that the Chief Wildlife Warden shall control, manage, and maintain all Sanctuaries in accordance with such management plans for the Sanctuary as are approved by the Chief Wildlife Warden in conformity with the guidelines issued by the Central Government.

Under Section 34(3) of the Act, no new licence under the Arms Act, 1959 can be granted within a radius of 10 km of a Sanctuary (and National Park under Section 35(8)) without the prior concurrence of the Chief Wildlife Warden. The 2022 Amendment inserted sub-section (4) into Section 34, providing that no renewal of any licence under the Arms Act, 1959 shall be granted to any person residing within 10 km of a Sanctuary except under intimation to the Chief Wildlife Warden or the authorised officer.

While Section 62A empowers the Central Government to regulate or prohibit the import, trade, possession, or proliferation of invasive alien species, Section 2(16A) (inserted by the 2022 Amendment) defines 'invasive alien species' strictly as 'a species of animal or plant which is not native to India and whose introduction or spread may threaten or adversely impact wildlife or its habitat'. Therefore, species native to one part of India that turn invasive in another part of India (such as Chital in the Andaman Islands) do not fall under this statutory definition.

ref: Sections 2(16A), 33, 34(3), 34(4) & 62A of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022)

stem: With reference to the institutional framework of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) and the State Boards for Wildlife (SBWL) under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended in 2022), consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the National Board for Wildlife is chaired by the Prime Minister, its Standing Committee is chaired by the Union Minister in charge of Environment, Forest and Climate Change.

2. Following the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, a State Board for Wildlife is statutorily empowered to constitute its own Standing Committee to exercise delegated powers at the state level.

3. A State Government can alter the boundaries of a Wildlife Sanctuary solely on the recommendation of the State Board for Wildlife, whereas the recommendation of the National Board for Wildlife is mandatory only for altering the boundaries of a National Park.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Sections 5A and 5B of the WPA, 1972, the Prime Minister chairs the plenary NBWL while the Union Environment Minister (Vice-Chairperson of NBWL) chairs its Standing Committee. The 2022 Amendment inserted Section 6B to allow State Boards for Wildlife to also constitute Standing Committees, while both Sanctuaries (Section 26A) and National Parks (Section 35) require the NBWL's recommendation for any boundary alteration.

exp.why: Under Section 5A of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the Prime Minister is the Chairperson of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) and the Union Minister in charge of Forests and Wildlife is its Vice-Chairperson. Under Section 5B, the Standing Committee of the NBWL is chaired by the Vice-Chairperson of the NBWL (the Union Environment Minister).

The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 inserted Section 6B into the principal Act, empowering every State Board for Wildlife (SBWL) to constitute a Standing Committee—chaired by the Vice-Chairperson of the SBWL (the State Minister in charge of Forests and Wildlife) and comprising the Member-Secretary and up to ten nominated members of the SBWL—to perform duties delegated to it.

Under Section 26A(3) (for Wildlife Sanctuaries) as well as Section 35(5) (for National Parks) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, no alteration of the boundaries of either a Sanctuary or a National Park can be made by the State Government except on a recommendation of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL).

ref: Sections 5A, 5B, 6, 6B, 26A(3) & 35(5) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the integration of ex-situ and in-situ wildlife conservation in India:
items: Statement-I: Under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the Central Zoo Authority (CZA) is statutorily empowered to identify endangered species of wild animals for concerted captive breeding and assign responsibility for their propagation to designated zoos and conservation breeding centres for eventual wild reintroduction.

Statement-II: Under Section 38I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, recognized zoos and conservation breeding centres are legally barred from acquiring, transferring, or exchanging any wild animal listed in Schedule I of the Act.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Section 38C of the WPA, 1972, the Central Zoo Authority coordinates off-display conservation breeding of endangered species (such as Pygmy Hog, Red Panda, Vultures, and Great Indian Bustard) to supplement wild populations in National Parks and Sanctuaries. Section 38I explicitly permits zoos and CZA-approved conservation breeding centres to acquire or transfer Schedule I and Schedule II animals with the prior permission of the CZA.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Under Section 38C(d) and (g) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the Central Zoo Authority (CZA) is mandated to identify endangered species of wild animals for captive breeding, assign responsibility in this regard to designated coordinating and participating zoos/conservation breeding centres, and ensure the maintenance of studbooks to maintain genetic diversity for eventual wild reintroduction.

Statement-II is incorrect. Section 38I(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 does not impose an absolute ban; rather, it provides that a recognized zoo may acquire, sell, or transfer any wild animal or captive animal specified in Schedules I and II with the 'previous permission of the Central Zoo Authority'. Furthermore, the proviso to Section 38I(2) specifically exempts CZA-approved conservation breeding centres and rescue centres from the restriction of transacting only with recognized zoos, enabling them to receive founder stock and reintroduce bred animals into Protected Areas.

ref: Sections 38C & 38I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972; Central Zoo Authority Guidelines on Conservation Breeding

stem: With reference to the ecological and statutory profile of coastal and island Biosphere Reserves in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve encompasses both Campbell Bay National Park and Galathea National Park as its core zones and is drained by the perennial Galathea River.

2. The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve comprises a chain of twenty-one low-lying islands and adjacent shallow coastal waters between Rameswaram and Thoothukudi, supporting seagrass beds that serve as a critical foraging ground for the Dugong.

3. Both the Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve and the Similipal Biosphere Reserve are included in the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves, and each contains a notified National Park as well as a Tiger Reserve.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's coastal and island Biosphere Reserves integrate multiple statutory Protected Area designations (National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, and Tiger Reserves) within a wider landscape zoning model. Great Nicobar BR (containing Campbell Bay NP and Galathea NP), Gulf of Mannar BR (21 coral islands and seagrass beds), Sundarbans BR, and Similipal BR are all recognized under UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.

exp.why: The Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve (included in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves in 2013) covers roughly 85% of Great Nicobar Island and incorporates two core National Parks: Campbell Bay National Park in the north and Galathea National Park in the south. It is drained by the perennial Galathea River, whose mouth at Galathea Bay is one of the most important nesting sites in the Indian Ocean for the Giant Leatherback sea turtle, and its tropical wet evergreen forests harbour the endemic Nicobar megapode.

The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve (designated in 1989 and included in UNESCO's WNBR in 2001) spans a chain of 21 islands and adjoining coral reefs, estuaries, and shallow coastal waters from Rameswaram to Thoothukudi (Tuticorin) in Tamil Nadu. Its extensive seagrass meadows form the prime foraging habitat for the vulnerable marine mammal Dugong (Dugong dugon).

Both the Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve (West Bengal, inducted into UNESCO WNBR in 2001) and the Similipal Biosphere Reserve (Odisha, located near the eastern coastal plains in Mayurbhanj and inducted into UNESCO WNBR in 2009) are part of UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves, and each encompasses both a notified National Park (Sundarbans NP; Similipal NP) and a notified Tiger Reserve (Sundarbans TR; Similipal TR).

ref: MoEFCC Biosphere Reserves Division; UNESCO Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme Directory

stem: Situated on the high-altitude Tibetan plateau extension in the Trans-Himalayan biogeographic zone, this Protected Area encompasses high-altitude brackish and oligotrophic wetlands such as Tso Moriri and Pangong Tso. Its cold desert steppe vegetation supports the Tibetan Wild Ass (Kiang), Tibetan Gazelle, and breeding populations of the Black-necked Crane, while its rangelands are traditionally grazed by semi-nomadic pastoralists who rear Pashmina-producing goats. Which of the following Protected Areas is described in the passage above?
core: Changthang Cold Desert Wildlife Sanctuary in Ladakh represents the Trans-Himalayan Tibetan Plateau biome containing high-altitude lakes (Tso Moriri, Pangong Tso, Tso Kar), flagship fauna like the Kiang and Black-necked Crane, and traditional Changpa pastoralists.

exp.why: Option (D) is correct because the Changthang Cold Desert Wildlife Sanctuary (located in the Ladakhi Changthang plateau) encompasses the high-altitude wetlands of Tso Moriri, Pangong Tso, and Tso Kar. Its cold desert steppe and alpine marshes provide critical breeding habitat for the Black-necked Crane (Grus nigricollis), Tibetan Wild Ass (Kiang), Tibetan Gazelle (Goa), and Snow Leopard, while supporting the semi-nomadic Changpa pastoralist community known for rearing Changra (Pashmina) goats. Option (A) Pin Valley National Park and Option (C) Kibber Wildlife Sanctuary are located in the Spiti Valley of Himachal Pradesh (famous for Snow Leopard and Siberian Ibex) and do not contain Tso Moriri or Pangong Tso. Option (B) Hemis National Park lies south of the Indus River in Ladakh and is renowned for dry alpine steppes housing the Snow Leopard, Argali, and Ladakh Urial (Shapu), rather than the brackish lacustrine basins of the Changthang plateau.

ref: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) Biogeographic Classification of India; MoEFCC Protected Area Network Directory

stem: Consider the following statutory stages involved in constituting an area (not comprised within any Reserve Forest or the territorial waters) as a Wildlife Sanctuary under Chapter IV of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972:
items: 1. Publication of a proclamation by the Collector in the regional language in every town and village in or in the neighbourhood of the area requiring any person claiming any right to prefer a written claim within two months.
2. Issuance of an initial notification by the State Government declaring its intention to constitute the area as a Sanctuary.

3. Passing of an order by the Collector either excluding the claimed land from the limits of the proposed Sanctuary, proceeding to acquire the rights, or allowing the continuation of rights in consultation with the Chief Wildlife Warden.
4. Issuance of a notification by the State Government specifying the final limits of the area and declaring that it shall be a Sanctuary on and from a specified date.
prompt: What is the correct chronological sequence of the above statutory stages under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972?
core: For non-reserve forest lands, constituting a Wildlife Sanctuary follows a strict statutory progression under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972: declaration of intention (Section 18), Collector's proclamation (Section 21), inquiry and settlement/continuation of rights (Sections 22-24), and final notification (Section 26A). In contrast, Reserve Forests and territorial waters bypass the Collector's inquiry process and are directly notified under Section 26A(1)(b).

exp.why: Stage 1 corresponds to Section 21 of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Within 60 days of the State Government's declaration of intention under Section 18, the Collector must publish a proclamation in the regional language requiring claimants to submit written claims specifying the nature and extent of their rights and compensation details within two months. Hence, it is the second step in the chronological sequence.

Stage 2 corresponds to Section 18(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, where the State Government initiates the process for land not comprised within any reserve forest or territorial waters by declaring its intention to constitute such area as a Sanctuary. Hence, it is the first step in the chronological sequence.

Stage 3 corresponds to Section 24(2) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Following the inquiry into claims under Section 22, the Collector passes an order admitting or rejecting the claim and, if admitted, either excludes the land from the proposed sanctuary, proceeds to acquire the right, or—in consultation with the Chief Wildlife Warden under Section 24(2)(c)—allows the continuation of any right inside a Sanctuary (a provision absent in National Parks). Hence, it is the third step in the sequence.

Stage 4 corresponds to Section 26A(1)(a) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Once the two-month claim period has elapsed and all claims have been disposed of by the Collector, the State Government issues the final notification declaring the area a Sanctuary. Notably, if the area is already a Reserve Forest or part of territorial waters, rights have already been settled or are governed separately, allowing direct notification under Section 26A(1)(b) without going through the Section 18–25 Collector inquiry process.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Sections 18, 21, 22, 24, and 26A

stem: With reference to the inclusion of territorial waters within a Wildlife Sanctuary or a National Park under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, consider the following statements:
items: 1. A State Government can include any part of the territorial waters in a Wildlife Sanctuary or a National Park only after obtaining the prior concurrence of the Central Government.

2. The maritime limits of the territorial waters to be included in a Sanctuary are statutorily determined by the State Board for Wildlife in consultation with the Director General of the Indian Coast Guard.

3. While determining the limits of territorial waters to be included in a Sanctuary, the Act explicitly mandates that adequate measures shall be taken to protect the occupational interests of local fishermen, and once notified, no alteration of the boundaries of the Sanctuary can be made by the State Government except on a recommendation of the National Board for Wild Life.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Provisos to Section 26A(1) and Section 26A(3) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, including territorial waters in a Protected Area requires prior Central Government concurrence, boundary determination in consultation with the Chief Naval Hydrographer, protection of local fishermen's occupational interests, and National Board for Wild Life recommendation for any subsequent boundary alteration.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Because territorial waters (up to 12 nautical miles from the baseline) fall under the sovereign jurisdiction of the Union, the first proviso to Section 26A(1) (for Sanctuaries) and the proviso to Section 35(1) (for National Parks) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 explicitly stipulate that prior concurrence of the Central Government must be obtained by the State Government before including any part of the territorial waters in a Sanctuary or National Park.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under the second proviso to Section 26A(1) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the limits of the area of the territorial waters to be included in the Sanctuary shall be determined in consultation with the Chief Naval Hydrographer of the Central Government, not the State Board for Wildlife in consultation with the Director General of the Indian Coast Guard.

Statement 3 is correct. The second proviso to Section 26A(1) mandates that the limits of the territorial waters to be included in the Sanctuary shall be determined after taking adequate measures to protect the occupational interests of the local fishermen. Furthermore, under Section 26A(3), no alteration of the boundaries of a Sanctuary shall be made by the State Government except on a recommendation of the National Board for Wild Life.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, Section 26A(1) Provisos, Section 26A(3), and Section 35(1)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs) in India:
items: Statement-I: The designation of a wetland or forest habitat as an Important Bird and Biodiversity Area (IBA) in India does not by itself enforce legal restrictions on land use or confer statutory protection upon the site.

Statement-II: In India, Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs) are identified by the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) and BirdLife International as an independent civil-society scientific inventory based on standardized global ornithological criteria, outside the statutory framework of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs) are scientifically identified priority conservation sites curated by BirdLife International and the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) in India using global ornithological criteria; because it is an NGO-led scientific inventory outside domestic legislation, the IBA label confers no automatic statutory protection unless separately notified under Indian law.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Identifying a habitat as an Important Bird and Biodiversity Area (IBA) in India does not automatically confer legal status, land-use restrictions, or statutory protection unless the site is separately notified by the Government as a National Park, Wildlife Sanctuary, Conservation Reserve, Community Reserve, Ramsar Wetland, or Biodiversity Heritage Site.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The IBA programme is a non-governmental global scientific initiative coordinated by BirdLife International and implemented in India through its partner organization, the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), using four standardized quantitative criteria (A1: Globally threatened species; A2: Restricted-range endemic species; A3: Biome-restricted assemblages; A4: Large congregations). Because it is an independent civil-society scientific prioritization exercise rather than a legislative notification under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, it lacks autonomous statutory enforceability.

ref: BNHS-India & BirdLife International: Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas in India; Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972

stem: With reference to the application of Island Biogeography Theory and landscape ecology to Protected Area network design, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: A single large continuous Protected Area generally sustains more viable populations of interior forest-specialist species with lower local extinction risk than several small isolated habitat patches of equivalent total area, unless those patches are linked by functional wildlife corridors.

Statement-II: Fragmenting a continuous habitat into smaller isolated patches reduces the overall perimeter-to-area ratio, thereby suppressing microclimatic fluctuations and invasive weed proliferation along reserve boundaries.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Habitat fragmentation increases the perimeter-to-area ratio (edge-to-interior ratio), intensifying deleterious edge effects (microclimatic stress, invasive species, human-wildlife conflict) and genetic drift in small isolated patches; functional wildlife corridors counteract this by restoring gene flow and demographic rescue across a metapopulation.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Based on MacArthur and Wilson's Theory of Island Biogeography and metapopulation dynamics, interior forest-specialist and wide-ranging apex species suffer high local extinction rates in small isolated patches due to inbreeding depression, demographic stochasticity, and diminished core habitat. Functional wildlife corridors mitigate fragmentation by enabling dispersal, gene flow, and the 'rescue effect' between subpopulations.

Statement-II is incorrect because subdividing a large continuous habitat into several smaller patches geometrically increases (not reduces) the total perimeter-to-area ratio. A higher perimeter-to-area ratio exposes a much larger proportion of the Protected Area to adverse 'edge effects'—including elevated temperature fluctuations, desiccation by wind, lower humidity, colonization by heliophilic invasive weeds (such as Lantana camara and Parthenium), nest parasitism, and escalated human-wildlife conflict—while drastically shrinking the undisturbed core interior habitat.

ref: MacArthur & Wilson's Theory of Island Biogeography; WII Guidelines on Eco-Friendly Linear Infrastructure & Wildlife Corridors

stem: Under Target 3 ('30 by 30' target) of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), countries account for both formal 'Protected Areas' and 'Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures' (OECMs). In this context, what is the fundamental defining distinction between a formal Protected Area and an OECM?

opts.A: Protected Areas are notified exclusively in terrestrial and inland wetland ecosystems, whereas OECMs are designated exclusively for coastal and high-seas marine ecosystems.
opts.B: While a Protected Area must have nature conservation as its dedicated primary management objective, an OECM achieves sustained long-term outcomes for in-situ conservation of biodiversity regardless of whether conservation is its primary management objective.
opts.C: Protected Areas can be governed only by sovereign government agencies, whereas OECMs can be governed only by private corporations and urban local bodies.
opts.D: Unlike Protected Areas which conserve wild habitats in-situ, OECMs encompass ex-situ conservation institutions such as botanical gardens, seed banks, and zoological parks.

core: Adopted under CBD Decision 14/8 and integrated into Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, an OECM is a geographically defined area outside Protected Areas that delivers effective, long-term in-situ biodiversity conservation as a primary, secondary, or ancillary outcome of its management.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. According to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD Decision 14/8) and IUCN-WCPA guidelines, a formal Protected Area must have the conservation of nature as its explicit primary management objective. In contrast, an 'Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measure' (OECM) is a geographically defined area other than a Protected Area which is governed and managed in ways that achieve positive and sustained long-term outcomes for the in-situ conservation of biodiversity, regardless of whether nature conservation is its primary objective (for example, sacred groves, watershed protection forests, military cantonment buffers, or sustainably managed agro-biodiversity estates where conservation is achieved as a secondary or ancillary outcome). Option (A) is incorrect as both Protected Areas and OECMs apply across terrestrial, inland water, and marine realms. Option (C) is incorrect as both Protected Areas and OECMs can exist under four governance types (government, shared, private, or indigenous/local communities). Option (D) is incorrect because OECMs are strictly in-situ area-based conservation spaces, not ex-situ facilities.

ref: CBD Decision 14/8; Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework Target 3; MoEFCC-NBA-UNDP India OECM Guidelines

stem: Despite a steady rise in the population of the Asiatic Lion (Panthera leo persica) and its natural dispersal into satellite agro-pastoral habitats across the Greater Gir landscape in the Saurashtra peninsula, why do wildlife epidemiologists and conservation biologists strongly emphasize establishing a geographically disjunct free-ranging population outside Gujarat?
prompt: Select the most appropriate ecological and genetic reason from the options given below:

opts.A: The dry deciduous teak forests of Gir are rapidly transforming into sub-alpine montane grasslands due to regional microclimatic shifts, inducing fatal high-altitude thermal stress in lions.
opts.B: A single contiguous metapopulation exhibiting high genetic homozygosity from a historic population bottleneck remains critically vulnerable to stochastic mass mortality from virulent epizootics such as Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) and Babesiosis.
opts.C: Unlike African lions, Asiatic lions possess a prominent longitudinal abdominal skin fold and bifurcated infraorbital foramina that physiologically prevent them from hunting medium-sized ungulates outside closed-canopy teak forests.
opts.D: Under the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, any Schedule I carnivore whose single-state population exceeds five hundred individuals must be statutorily translocated across at least three distinct biogeographic zones.

core: The entire wild population of the Asiatic Lion is currently confined to a single interconnected metapopulation in the Saurashtra landscape of Gujarat, descended from a severe late-19th-century genetic bottleneck that resulted in low major histocompatibility complex (MHC) diversity. Establishing an independent, geographically isolated second population (such as in Kuno National Park) is an epidemiological insurance strategy against a single outbreak of Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) or tick-borne Babesiosis wiping out the subspecies.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct: Asiatic lions underwent a severe genetic bottleneck in the late 19th and early 20th centuries when their numbers dropped to fewer than a few dozen individuals in Gir. Consequently, the surviving Saurashtra metapopulation exhibits high genetic homozygosity and reduced immunological diversity. Even though lions have dispersed into satellite habitats (Mitiyala, Girnar, Paniya, coastal corridors), these sub-populations remain epidemiologically linked through dispersing males and shared feral dog/livestock reservoirs. In 2018, a combined outbreak of Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) and protozoan Babesiosis killed over two dozen lions in Gir, mirroring the 1994 Serengeti CDV epizootic that wiped out 30% of the local African lion population. Hence, conservation biology mandates a geographically separate population (such as Kuno in Madhya Pradesh) as insurance against single-event stochastic extinction. Option (A) is incorrect because Gir is a low-elevation dry deciduous and thorn scrub ecosystem with no sub-alpine transformation. Option (C) is incorrect because although a longitudinal abdominal skin fold, sparser mane, and bifurcated infraorbital foramen are genuine morphological markers distinguishing Asiatic from African lions, they do not impair hunting in open or agro-pastoral landscapes. Option (D) is incorrect because no such statutory threshold exists in the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

ref: Supreme Court Judgment in Centre for Environmental Law, WWF-India v. Union of India (2013); WII Asiatic Lion Conservation Project Reports

stem: With reference to the ecology, habitat range, and evolutionary genetics of the Royal Bengal Tiger (Panthera tigris tigris) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In India, wild tigers demonstrate broad ecological plasticity, inhabiting landscapes ranging from the intertidal halophytic mangroves of the Sundarbans to high-altitude temperate and sub-alpine forests above 3,600 metres in the Eastern Himalayas.

2. The pseudo-melanistic ('black') tigers documented in the Similipal Tiger Reserve of Odisha represent a distinct, reproductively isolated subspecies of Panthera tigris uniquely adapted to moist deciduous sal forests.

3. The coalesced dark stripe phenotype of Similipal's pseudo-melanistic tigers is caused by a single base-pair autosomal recessive mutation in the Transmembrane Aminopeptidase Q (Taqpep) gene, sustained in high frequency by genetic drift and inbreeding in an isolated population.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Royal Bengal Tiger exhibits remarkable habitat adaptability across India, spanning sea-level mangrove swamps to snow-bound Eastern Himalayan valleys above 3,600 m. The rare 'black' or pseudo-melanistic tigers of Similipal Tiger Reserve are not a separate subspecies, but standard Bengal tigers carrying an autosomal recessive point mutation in the Taqpep gene whose frequency increased due to geographic isolation and genetic drift.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The Royal Bengal Tiger occupies an extraordinary range of biomes in India—from the tidal mangrove swamps of the Sundarbans at sea level, dry thorn forests of Ranthambore, and alluvial Terai grasslands of Kaziranga-Corbett, up to high-altitude temperate and alpine zones exceeding 3,600–4,000 metres in Dibang Valley (Arunachal Pradesh), Pangolakha (Sikkim), and Neora Valley (West Bengal).

Statement 2 is incorrect: Similipal's pseudo-melanistic tigers are not a separate subspecies; they belong to the same mainland subspecies (Panthera tigris tigris) and freely interbreed with normal-colored orange tigers within Similipal.

Statement 3 is correct: Genomic research by the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS) demonstrated that pseudo-melanism in Similipal tigers—where thick black stripes widen and fuse over the tawny background coat—results from a single nucleotide mutation (cytosine to thymine transition) in the Transmembrane Aminopeptidase Q (Taqpep) gene. Because Similipal has minimal functional corridor connectivity with other Central Indian tiger landscapes, a small founder size, genetic drift, and inbreeding have elevated the frequency of this recessive allele.

ref: NCBS-WII Study on Similipal Pseudo-Melanistic Tigers (PNAS, 2021); NTCA Status of Tigers in India Report

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the physiology and ecology of the Snow Leopard (Panthera uncia):
items: Statement-I: Unlike other members of the genus Panthera, the Snow Leopard survives extreme Trans-Himalayan winters by entering prolonged metabolic hibernation in sub-nivean burrows and possesses thick fibro-elastic vocal fold pads that enable it to produce a long-distance territorial roar.

Statement-II: The Snow Leopard possesses enlarged nasal cavities that warm cold thin mountain air before it reaches the lungs, a long thick tail that functions both as a dynamic counterbalance on steep rocky cliffs and as a thermal wrap during rest, and a close predator-prey coupling with high-altitude ungulates such as the Bharal (Blue Sheep) and Asiatic Ibex.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Although phylogenetically classified inside the genus Panthera, the Snow Leopard cannot roar because its larynx lacks the specialized thick layers of fibro-elastic tissue found in lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards. It does not hibernate in winter; instead, it relies on specialized cold-arid morphological adaptations and tracks seasonal altitudinal migrations of wild caprids like Bharal and Asiatic Ibex.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect on both physiological counts: First, Snow Leopards do not hibernate; they remain active year-round across the cold arid Trans-Himalayan steppes and alpine zones ( typically between 3,000 and 5,500 metres), descending only slightly to lower elevations in winter following their wild ungulate prey. Second, despite belonging to the genus Panthera, the Snow Leopard is the only Panthera species that cannot roar. While it has an incompletely ossified hyoid apparatus, its vocal folds lack the thick, specialized fibro-elastic pads required to generate the low-frequency, high-amplitude roar characteristic of lions, tigers, leopards, and jaguars.

Statement-II is correct: The Snow Leopard shows classic evolutionary adaptations to high-altitude hypoxia and freezing temperatures—including enlarged paranasal sinuses/nasal cavities to pre-warm chilled dry air, wide fur-covered paws acting as natural snowshoes to reduce foot-loading on snow, small rounded ears to minimize radiative heat loss, and a muscular tail nearly equal to its body length used for agile balance while pursuing Bharal (Pseudois nayaur) and Asiatic Ibex (Capra sibirica) across precipitous crags as well as a facial muffler against sub-zero winds.

ref: Project Snow Leopard (MoEFCC); Snow Leopard Population Assessment in India (SPAI) Report by WII

stem: With reference to the Clouded Leopard (Neofelis nebulosa) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Among all living felids, it possesses the longest upper canine teeth relative to its skull size and has specialized, supinatable hind ankle joints that allow it to descend vertical tree trunks head-first.
2. In India, its largest natural populations are found in the montane Shola-grassland ecosystems of the Southern Western Ghats, where it co-occurs with the Nilgiri Tahr.
3. Because it is phylogenetically classified as a canopy-dwelling subspecies of the Indian Leopard (Panthera pardus fusca), it is placed under Schedule II of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Clouded Leopard (Neofelis nebulosa) is an evolutionary basal member of the Pantherinae subfamily—distinct from the genus Panthera—characterized by extraordinary arboreal biomechanics and saber-like upper canines relative to skull size. In India, its distribution is restricted to the tropical and subtropical evergreen and moist deciduous forests of the Eastern Himalayas and Northeast India, and it is protected under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The Clouded Leopard has the longest upper canines relative to skull size of any extant felid (often compared convergently to primitive saber-toothed cats) and a wide gape (~100 degrees). Furthermore, its flexible fibula-tibia and hind ankle joints can rotate (supinate) up to 180 degrees, enabling it to grip bark and climb down vertical trunks head-first, hang upside down from branches by its hind feet, and leap across forest canopies.

Statement 2 is incorrect: In India, the Clouded Leopard is completely absent from the Western Ghats and Peninsular India. Its geographic range is restricted to the Eastern Himalayas (Sikkim, northern West Bengal) and the hill states of Northeast India—notably Dampa Tiger Reserve (Mizoram), Namdapha and Pakke (Arunachal Pradesh), Manas (Assam), Balpakram-Nokrek (Meghalaya, where it is the State Animal), and Sepahijala (Tripura).

Statement 3 is incorrect: The Clouded Leopard is not a subspecies of Panthera pardus; it belongs to a separate genus (Neofelis) that diverged at the base of the Pantherinae clade millions of years ago. Moreover, it is categorized as 'Vulnerable' on the IUCN Red List and is accorded the highest level of statutory protection under Schedule I (not Schedule II) of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended in 2022).

ref: WII Species Recovery Programme for Clouded Leopard; Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 Schedule I

stem: Consider the following pairs of India's lesser wild felids and their characteristic ecological niches and adaptations:
items: 1. Fishing Cat (Prionailurus viverrinus) : Inhabits estuarine mangroves and floodplain marshes such as Chilika and Coringa; possesses partially webbed front toes and a water-resistant layered coat
2. Caracal (Caracal caracal) : Inhabits high-altitude cold arid rocky steppes of Ladakh and Sikkim; flattens its low-set rounded ears to ambush pikas and mountain voles among boulders

3. Pallas's Cat (Otocolobus manul) : Inhabits semi-arid thorny scrublands and dry ravines of Kutch and Ranthambore; uses elongated black ear tufts and powerful hindlimbs to flush and intercept birds in mid-air

4. Rusty-Spotted Cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus) : Inhabits dry deciduous forests, scrublands, and rocky hillocks of Peninsular and Western India; an agile nocturnal arboreal hunter and one of the world's smallest wild cats
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: India hosts the highest diversity of wild felids in the world (15 species), each partitioned into highly specialized biomes: the Fishing Cat in coastal mangroves and inland reedbeds, the Caracal in western arid thorn scrub, Pallas's Cat in cold Trans-Himalayan alpine deserts, and the tiny Rusty-Spotted Cat across dry deciduous and rocky landscapes.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched: The Fishing Cat (State Animal of West Bengal and ambassador of Chilika Lake) is a wetland specialist occurring in the Sundarbans, Coringa mangroves (Andhra Pradesh), Bhitarkanika, Chilika, and Terai-Gangetic floodplains. It features partially webbed forepaws, claw sheaths that do not fully retract (aiding grip on slippery aquatic prey), and a dense, layered water-resistant coat.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched: The habitat and adaptation described belong to Pallas's Cat (Otocolobus manul), not the Caracal. The Caracal is a slender, long-legged felid restricted in India to the arid and semi-arid thorn scrub, ravines, and dry deciduous tracts of Kutch (Gujarat), Rajasthan (Ranthambore, Sariska), and parts of Madhya Pradesh.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched: The habitat and avian-hunting adaptation (long black ear tufts controlled by complex auricular muscles and explosive vertical leaps to catch flying birds) belong to the Caracal (Caracal caracal). Pallas's Cat (Otocolobus manul) is a stocky, dense-furred cold-desert felid inhabiting the high-altitude Trans-Himalayan steppes of Ladakh and northern Sikkim, notable for its low-set rounded ears and circular pupils (unlike the vertical slit pupils of most small cats).

Pair 4 is correctly matched: The Rusty-Spotted Cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus), weighing only 1.0 to 1.6 kg in adulthood, rivals the African Black-footed Cat as the world's smallest wild cat.
