Endemic to India, Sri Lanka, and the Nepal Terai, it primarily inhabits dry deciduous forests, scrub-jungles, bamboo thickets, and rocky outcrops across Peninsular, Central, and Western India.

ref: WII 'Small Cats of India' Monograph; IUCN Cat Specialist Group Assessments

stem: With reference to the Greater One-Horned Rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) and its floodplain habitat ecology in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It is an obligate megaherbivore of the alluvial Terai-Duar savanna grasslands and riverine marshes distributed along the Himalayan foothills and the Brahmaputra-Ganga floodplains.

2. In the Kaziranga landscape, annual monsoon flooding by the Brahmaputra River acts as a constructive ecological disturbance that flushes out choking aquatic weeds, deposits fertile silt, and arrests natural succession from tall wet grasslands into closed-canopy woodlands.
3. Pronounced sexual dimorphism in the species is characterized by the presence of two keratinous nasal horns in adult males and a single horn in adult females.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Greater One-Horned Rhinoceros is ecologically tied to early-successional tall alluvial grasslands (Saccharum-Phragmites complexes) and oxbow wetlands in the Terai-Duar and Brahmaputra floodplains. Annual riverine flooding is essential to prevent woodland encroachment and maintain these grazing meadows, while both sexes of the Indian species possess only a single keratinous horn.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: The Greater One-Horned Rhinoceros is the most semi-aquatic and grass-dependent of all living rhino species, thriving in the alluvial Terai-Duar savanna and floodplain grasslands (dominated by Saccharum spontaneum, Imperata cylindrica, and Arundo donax) across protected areas in Assam (Kaziranga, Pobitora, Orang, Manas), West Bengal (Jaldapara, Gorumara), and Uttar Pradesh (Dudhwa).

Statement 2 is correct: Although extreme flood peaks cause short-term wildlife mortality, seasonal monsoon inundation by the Brahmaputra is indispensable to the long-term survival of Kaziranga's rhinos. The floodwaters clear invasive water hyacinth (Pontederia crassipes) from beels (oxbow wetlands), replenish nutrient-rich alluvial silt, and inhibit woody tree seedlings from colonizing open meadows—thereby halting ecological succession that would otherwise turn the tall wet grasslands into ungrazeable woodland.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Both adult males and adult females of the Greater One-Horned Rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) as well as the Javan Rhinoceros (Rhinoceros sondaicus, where females often lack or have a minimal knob) belong to the single-horned genus Rhinoceros. In R. unicornis, both sexes carry a single black horn made of agglutinated keratin fibers lacking a bony core; two horns are found in the Sumatran, African White, and African Black rhinoceroses.

ref: Indian Rhino Vision 2020 (IRV 2020) Report; UNESCO World Heritage Site Dossier on Kaziranga National Park

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the demography and evolutionary biology of the Asian Elephant (Elephas maximus):
items: Statement-I: Historical selective poaching for ivory in Southern India caused a much sharper distortion in the adult male-to-female sex ratio of Asian Elephants than that typically observed in poached populations of African Bush Elephants (Loxodonta africana).
Statement-II: In Asian Elephants, prominent ivory tusks are sexually dimorphic and restricted exclusively to males, whereas both males and females develop prominent tusks in African Bush Elephants.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: In Asian Elephants (Elephas maximus), only males bear prominent ivory tusks while females are tuskless (or possess tiny non-protruding tushes), whereas both sexes carry tusks in African Bush Elephants. Consequently, ivory poaching in Asian Elephant landscapes selectively removes breeding bulls, severely skewing adult sex ratios and increasing the genetic proportion of tuskless males (makhnas).

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. During the late 20th century, rampant ivory poaching in landscapes such as the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (Periyar, Mudumalai, Bandipur) selectively targeted adult male Asian Elephants, resulting in highly skewed adult sex ratios (sometimes exceeding 1 adult male to 50-100 adult females) and artificially selecting for tuskless males ('makhnas'). In contrast, ivory poaching in Africa targets both adult males and older females with large tusks.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Elongated upper second incisors (tusks) are a sexually dimorphic trait in Elephas maximus: only males develop true tusks, whereas females lack tusks (or have small vestigial 'tushes' that barely protrude past the lip line). In Loxodonta africana, both sexes possess large ivory tusks, distributing poaching mortality across both males and females.

ref: MoEFCC Project Elephant Reports; IUCN SSC Asian Elephant Specialist Group; Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 (Schedule I)

stem: With reference to the ecology and conservation of the Gangetic River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Having evolved in highly turbid alluvial rivers, it lacks a crystalline eye lens and relies on continuous ultrasonic echolocation clicks to navigate and forage.
2. Although primarily riverine during the monsoon, adult females undertake seasonal migrations into the hypersaline pelagic waters of the Bay of Bengal for winter calving.
3. Its natural range is restricted to the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu river systems, where irrigation barrages have fragmented its metapopulation into isolated subpopulations.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Gangetic River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica) is an obligate freshwater cetacean endemic to the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu river basins. Adapted to silt-laden waters with near-zero visibility, it has lost its crystalline eye lens (detecting only light direction) and navigates via high-frequency biosonar, making it acutely vulnerable to acoustic pollution and physical fragmentation by river barrages.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Due to millions of years of adaptation to muddy, sediment-heavy Himalayan rivers where light penetration is minimal, the Gangetic River Dolphin has vestigial eyes lacking a crystalline lens. Its eyes function merely as light-direction sensors, and the animal swims on its side while emitting continuous ultrasonic echolocation clicks to map riverbeds and capture prey.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Gangetic River Dolphin is an obligate freshwater cetacean and never enters marine or hypersaline pelagic waters of the Bay of Bengal. During the monsoon it disperses upstream into smaller tributaries and returns to deeper main-stem river channels and counter-current eddy pools in winter and summer.

Statement 3 is correct. Platanista gangetica occurs solely in the Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna and Karnaphuli-Sangu basins across India, Nepal, and Bangladesh. Low-gated irrigation barrages (such as Farakka, Kosi, Gandak, and Narora) block upstream movement, isolating subpopulations and reducing genetic diversity.

ref: Project Dolphin (MoEFCC); Wildlife Institute of India Cetacean Action Plan; WPA 1972 (Schedule I)

stem: Consider the following statements comparing the Irrawaddy Dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris) and the Indus River Dolphin (Platanista minor):
items: 1. Like the Gangetic and Indus river dolphins, the Irrawaddy Dolphin possesses an elongated, narrow tooth-lined beak (rostrum) and lacks functional eyesight.
2. Unlike the Indus River Dolphin which is an obligate freshwater species, the Irrawaddy Dolphin is a euryhaline species capable of inhabiting brackish coastal lagoons and mangrove estuaries.
3. In India, naturally occurring resident populations of the Indus River Dolphin are found across the Satluj, Ravi, and Chenab river stretches in Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Indus River Dolphin (Platanista minor) is a functionally blind, long-snouted obligate freshwater platanistid restricted in India to the lower Beas River in Punjab, the Irrawaddy Dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris) is an oceanic delphinid with a blunt, beakless rounded head, functional eyesight, and euryhaline physiological adaptability to brackish lagoons like Chilika Lake and mangrove estuaries like the Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Irrawaddy Dolphin belongs to the family Delphinidae (oceanic dolphins) and is anatomically characterized by a high, rounded forehead (melon) with no distinct beak (rostrum) at all, a flexible neck, and fully functional eyesight. Only the true river dolphins of the genus Platanista (Gangetic and Indus dolphins) have long, pincer-like rostrums and lack crystalline eye lenses.

Statement 2 is correct. The Indus River Dolphin is strictly an obligate freshwater cetacean, whereas the Irrawaddy Dolphin is euryhaline—capable of tolerating a wide range of salinities—and thrives in brackish coastal lagoons (Chilika Lake in Odisha), mangrove estuaries (Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika), and freshwater river reaches in Southeast Asia.

Statement 3 is incorrect. In India, the surviving natural resident population of the Indus River Dolphin (Platanista minor) is confined exclusively to a 185-km stretch of the Beas River in Punjab (between Talwara and the Harike Barrage), having been extirpated from the upper reaches of other Indus tributaries due to irrigation barrages and water diversion.

ref: IUCN Red List Cetacean Assessments; WII Conservation Action Plan for Indus & Irrawaddy Dolphins

stem: With reference to the three native crocodilian species of India—Gharial (Gavialis gangeticus), Mugger (Crocodylus palustris), and Saltwater Crocodile (Crocodylus porosus)—consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Gharial is the most widely distributed crocodilian across peninsular Indian reservoirs and frequently undertakes overland migrations across dry terrain when seasonal ponds shrink during summer.
2. Adult male Gharials develop a bulbous cartilaginous nasal excrescence ('ghara') at the tip of the snout, which functions as an acoustic resonator and visual signal during courtship.

3. While the Mugger excavates deep burrows in riverbanks and lake margins to aestivate during severe summer heat, the Saltwater Crocodile possesses specialized lingual salt glands that allow it to osmoregulate in hyper-saline mangrove estuaries.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's three crocodilians exhibit distinct ecological niche partitioning: the Critically Endangered Gharial is an obligate fish-eater with weak limb musculature restricted to deep, fast-flowing northern rivers with sandbanks (Chambal, Girwa, Gandak, Ramganga); the Mugger is a broad-snouted generalist widespread across Indian lakes and rivers capable of walking overland and aestivating in burrows; and the Saltwater Crocodile is an estuarine apex predator equipped with lingual salt-excreting glands in Bhitarkanika, Sundarbans, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. It describes the behavioral ecology of the Mugger or Marsh Crocodile (Crocodylus palustris), not the Gharial. Adult Gharials lack the limb musculature required to lift their bellies off the ground for extended overland walking ('high walk'); they can only slide on wet sandbanks and are restricted to deep, flowing northern rivers (such as Chambal, Girwa, Ramganga, Gandak, and a tiny reintroduced population in the Mahanadi).

Statement 2 is correct. Sexually mature male Gharials develop a hollow, bulbous cartilaginous growth ('ghara', resembling an earthen pot) over their external nostrils. It modifies vocalizations into audible buzzing/hissing sounds, blows Underwater bubbles during courtship displays, and visually signals dominance.

Statement 3 is correct. Mugger crocodiles adapt to seasonal water scarcity and extreme temperatures in interior India by digging burrows along embankments for aestivation. Conversely, Saltwater Crocodiles (Crocodylus porosus) have specialized salt-secreting lingual glands on the tongue that excrete excess sodium and chloride ions, allowing them to thrive in coastal mangroves and marine environments without drinking fresh water.

ref: IUCN Crocodile Specialist Group; Indian Crocodile Conservation Project (1975); WPA 1972 (Schedule I)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Critically Endangered Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps):
items: Statement-I: The Great Indian Bustard experiences exceptionally high adult mortality from mid-air collisions with overhead high-voltage power transmission lines intersecting its arid and semi-arid grassland habitats.

Statement-II: Evolved for scanning open plains for terrestrial predators while foraging on the ground, the bird has laterally positioned eyes that provide wide panoramic side vision at the cost of a wide frontal blind spot in flight, compounded by its heavy body mass and low aerial maneuverability.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Great Indian Bustard's visual field is an evolutionary trade-off: laterally placed eyes provide a near-360-degree horizontal scan against ground predators in open short-grass plains while the head is tilted down foraging, leaving a blind spot directly ahead of the beak when the head is held in flight position. Combined with being one of the heaviest flying birds with high wing loading, it cannot detect or swerve around overhead transmission cables in time.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Overhead power transmission lines proliferating across renewable energy zones in the Thar landscape of Rajasthan and Kutch in Gujarat constitute the single largest direct anthropogenic cause of adult mortality for the Great Indian Bustard, prompting Supreme Court interventions (M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India) on undergrounding cables and installing bird diverters in priority habitats.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Sensory ecology studies show that bustards have minimal binocular frontal overlap; when flying with the head extended forward, the narrow binocular field points downward rather than straight ahead, creating a frontal blind spot. Because adult males weigh up to 15 kg with high wing loading, they lack the agility to execute last-second evasive maneuvers upon spotting cables.

ref: WII Great Indian Bustard Recovery Programme; Supreme Court Judgment in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI (2024)

stem: With reference to the Critically Endangered grassland and scrubland birds of India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Lesser Florican (Sypheotides indicus) breeds during the southwest monsoon in dry-zone savannas and agro-pastoral grasslands of western and central India, where males perform repetitive vertical aerial leaps above the grass canopy to attract mates.
2. The Bengal Florican (Houbaropsis bengalensis) is a strictly nocturnal cursorial bird endemic to the arid thorny scrub jungles of the Eastern Ghats.

3. Jerdon's Courser (Rhinoptilus bitorquatus) is a nocturnal ground-dwelling bird whose known wild range is confined to interspersed open patches within scrub forests in the Sri Lankamaleswara landscape of Andhra Pradesh.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's Critically Endangered open-ecosystem birds occupy distinct biogeographical niches: the Lesser Florican inhabits dry monsoon grasslands of western/central India (Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra); the Bengal Florican is a diurnal bustard restricted to wet alluvial Terai and Brahmaputra valley grasslands; and Jerdon's Courser is a strictly nocturnal plover-like bird endemic to thorny scrub jungles of the Eastern Ghats (Sri Lankamaleswara Wildlife Sanctuary).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The smallest of India's bustards, the Lesser Florican (Sypheotides indicus), congregates in dry savannas and grasslands (such as Shokaliya in Rajasthan, Blackbuck National Park Velavadar in Gujarat, and Sailana/Sardarpur in Madhya Pradesh) during the monsoon, where males leap up to 2 metres vertically into the air with a frog-like croaking rattle to advertise their territories.

Statement 2 is incorrect. It swaps the habitat and behavior of the Bengal Florican with Jerdon's Courser. The Bengal Florican (Houbaropsis bengalensis) is a diurnal bustard restricted to tall, wet alluvial grasslands (phantas and chaporis) of the Himalayan Terai arc (Dudhwa, Pilibhit) and the Brahmaputra valley (Manas, Kaziranga, Orang, D'Ering).

Statement 3 is correct. Jerdon's Courser (Rhinoptilus bitorquatus)—presumed extinct for 86 years until its rediscovery in 1986—is a strictly nocturnal, cursorial bird endemic to sparse, non-thorny and thorny scrubland patches in the Sri Lankamaleswara Wildlife Sanctuary (Kadapa basin) of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh.

ref: MoEFCC Species Recovery Programme; BNHS Grassland Avifauna Studies; WPA 1972 (Schedule I)

stem: This cervid is the only surviving native subspecies of the European Red Deer in the Indian subcontinent. Famous for the deep rutting roar of its stags during autumn and its impressive multi-tined antlers, the surviving wild population undertakes a critical seasonal altitudinal migration within the Zabarwan mountain range—spending harsh winters in lower oak-willow riverine valleys and ascending to upper birch and alpine meadows during summer. Today, its wild survival is severely threatened by a skewed female-to-male calf recruitment ratio, habitat fragmentation across its historical Sindh Valley corridors, and predation of fawns by feral dogs and leopards. Which one of the following species is described in the passage above?

opts.A: Swamp Deer (Barasingha) of Dudhwa and Kanha
opts.B: Shou (Sikkim Stag) of the Chumbi Valley
opts.C: Hangul (Kashmir Stag) of Dachigam National Park

core: The Hangul or Kashmir Stag (Cervus hanglu hanglu) is the sole surviving native subspecies of Red Deer in the Indian subcontinent, restricted primarily to Dachigam National Park and adjoining Tral-Overa-Aru corridors in Jammu and Kashmir. Its conservation is hindered by severe demographic bottlenecks, low fawn-to-hind ratios, and disruption of seasonal altitudinal migration between lower riverine forests and high-altitude alpine pastures.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct because the Hangul (Cervus hanglu hanglu), the UT animal of Jammu and Kashmir, is the only surviving Red Deer/Tarim Red Deer subspecies native to the Indian subcontinent. Its viable wild population is concentrated in Dachigam National Park in the Zabarwan range, where it migrates seasonally between lower riverine moist temperate forests (1,700–2,300 m) in winter and upper sub-alpine birch meadows (above 3,000 m) in summer. Option (A) is incorrect as the Barasingha (Rucervus duvaucelii) inhabits lowland terai swamps and central Indian hard-ground grasslands. Option (B) is incorrect because the Shou (Cervus wallichii) is distributed in southern Tibet and Bhutan with occasional sightings in Sikkim/Arunachal Pradesh, not the Zabarwan range. Option (D) is incorrect because the Sangai (Rucervus eldii eldii) is endemic to the floating phumdis of Loktak Lake in Manipur.

ref: IUCN Red List Assessment for Cervus hanglu ssp. hanglu; Wildlife Institute of India (WII) Hangul Recovery Programme Reports

stem: With reference to the ecology and conservation of the Sangai (Brow-antlered Deer) in Keibul Lamjao National Park, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Maintaining permanently high water levels year-round in Loktak Lake through the operation of the Ithai Barrage has progressively degraded the thickness and load-bearing capacity of the floating biomass mats (phumdis) that support the Sangai.

Statement-II: The floating phumdis require continuous year-round detachment from the mineral lakebed to absorb nutrients exclusively from the water column, whereas contact with bottom sediments during the dry season induces rapid anaerobic decay of their root matrices.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The survival of the Sangai (Rucervus eldii eldii) depends on the structural integrity of phumdis—heterogeneous floating mats of soil, organic matter, and vegetation in Loktak Lake. The natural hydrological cycle requires seasonal water drawdown in the dry winter months so that the phumdis sink and rest on the lakebed to replenish essential mineral nutrients.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. The commissioning of the Ithai Barrage for the Loktak Hydroelectric Project converted Loktak Lake from a pulsing wetland with natural seasonal water-level fluctuations into a permanently impounded reservoir. This permanent high water level has caused progressive thinning, fragmentation, and loss of buoyancy of the phumdis inside Keibul Lamjao National Park, threatening the Sangai (whose splayed pasterns are adapted to walk on thick floating mats).

Statement-II is incorrect because it reverses the ecological mechanism. In a natural hydrological regime, water levels in Loktak Lake recede during the dry season, allowing the floating phumdis to settle onto the mineral lakebed. This seasonal grounding enables the roots of mat-forming grasses and reeds (such as Zizania latifolia and Phragmites karka) to absorb vital mineral nutrients from bottom sediments, thickening and strengthening the mat before the monsoon re-floats it. Permanent inundation prevents this lakebed contact, starving the vegetation of mineral nutrients and causing the phumdis to thin and break apart.

ref: WII Conservation Action Plan for Sangai (Rucervus eldii eldii); Ramsar Sites Information Service: Loktak Lake (Montreux Record)

stem: With reference to the Nilgiri Tahr (Nilgiritragus hylocrius), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Its natural wild distribution extends continuously along the entire Western Ghats escarpment from the Tapti River valley in Gujarat down to Kanyakumari.
2. Unlike Himalayan mountain ungulates, it is primarily a closed-canopy browser that inhabits the dense interior of stunted Shola forests and avoids open montane grasslands.

3. Afforesting high-altitude montane grasslands in the Nilgiris and Anamalais with fast-growing exotic species such as Black Wattle (Acacia mearnsii) and Eucalyptus expands its winter foraging habitat.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Nilgiri Tahr is the only mountain ungulate in southern India, endemic to a narrow 400-km stretch of the Southern Western Ghats in Kerala and Tamil Nadu. It is an obligate grazer of high-altitude open montane wet grasslands flanking steep rocky cliffs, making woody invasion by exotic wattle, pine, and eucalyptus plantations one of its gravest habitat threats.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Nilgiri Tahr does not occur in the northern or central Western Ghats (Maharashtra, Goa, or Karnataka). In the wild, it is restricted to fragmented pockets along a narrow ~400 km stretch of the Southern Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu and Kerala (between the Nilgiri Hills in the north and the Ashambu/Kanyakumari Hills in the south), with Eravikulam National Park hosting the largest contiguous population.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Nilgiri Tahr is an obligate open-habitat grazer and mixed feeder that depends on high-altitude montane wet grasslands (1,200 to 2,600 metres elevation) interspersed with steep, precipitous rocky cliffs for predator detection and escape. It actively avoids the dense, closed-canopy interiors of Shola forests where ambush predators such as leopards and tigers have a hunting advantage.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Historical commercial planting and subsequent invasive spread of exotic woody species—particularly Black Wattle (Acacia mearnsii), Scotch Broom, Pines, and Eucalyptus—across the Nilgiri, Anamalai, and Palani hills have replaced native palatable montane grasses and obstructed predator sightlines, severely shrinking and fragmenting the viable habitat of the Nilgiri Tahr.

ref: Project Nilgiri Tahr (Tamil Nadu Forest Department); IUCN Red List Assessment for Nilgiritragus hylocrius

stem: With reference to the Lion-tailed Macaque (Macaca silenus), consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the wild, it is endemic only to the tropical wet evergreen forest belt of the Western Ghats across Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu.
2. It is a nocturnal, predominantly ground-dwelling primate that readily adapts to open-canopy tea estates when primary rainforests are cleared.
3. Throughout the southern Western Ghats, its foraging ecology is closely linked to the flowering and fruiting cycles of Cullenia exarillata, a dominant upper-canopy rainforest tree.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Lion-tailed Macaque is an Endangered, strictly diurnal and exclusively arboreal Old World monkey endemic to the upper canopy of tropical wet evergreen rainforests in the Western Ghats of Karnataka, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. Because it rarely descends to the forest floor, linear infrastructure and monoculture plantations that break upper-canopy continuity isolate its subpopulations.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In the wild, the Lion-tailed Macaque is strictly endemic only to the fragmented tropical wet evergreen rainforests (Shola and rainforest complexes) of the Western Ghats across three states: Karnataka (e.g., Sirsi-Honnavara, Kudremukh), Kerala (e.g., Silent Valley, Periyar), and Tamil Nadu (e.g., Kalakkad-Mundanthurai, Anamalai).

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Lion-tailed Macaque is strictly diurnal (active during the day) and almost exclusively arboreal, spending over 98% of its waking hours in the upper canopy of tall evergreen rainforests. Unlike the Bonnet Macaque or Rhesus Macaque, it is extremely shy of human habitation, avoids descending to the ground, and suffers severe demographic decline in treeless monoculture tea estates.

Statement 3 is correct. In the southern Western Ghats (such as Silent Valley and Kalakkad-Mundanthurai), the evergreen tree Cullenia exarillata serves as a keystone food species for the Lion-tailed Macaque, providing protein-rich seeds and fleshy spiny flowers during lean fruiting periods while the macaque aids in its pollination.

ref: schedule I, Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended in 2022); ENVIS Centre on Faunal Diversity (ZSI)

stem: Consider the following table regarding the taxonomy and biogeographical boundaries of primates native to India:
items: 1. Western Hoolock Gibbon : Tailless Lesser Ape : Restricted to forests north of the Brahmaputra River between the Sankosh and Manas rivers
2. Gee's Golden Langur : Colobine Old-World Monkey : Restricted to forests south of the Brahmaputra River and east of the Dibang River
3. Grey Slender Loris : Nocturnal Strepsirrhine Primate : Inhabits tropical scrub, thorn, and dry deciduous forests of Southern India including the Kadavur landscape
prompt: In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
core: Major Himalayan and Assam valley rivers act as strict zoogeographical barriers for arboreal primates in Northeast India: the Brahmaputra River separates the Golden Langur on the northern bank (bounded by the Sankosh and Manas rivers) from the Hoolock Gibbon on the southern bank. Meanwhile, the Grey Slender Loris is a nocturnal insectivorous strepsirrhine primate of southern India's dry deciduous and thorn scrub landscapes.

exp.why: Row 1 is incorrectly matched. While the Western Hoolock Gibbon (Hoolock hoolock) is indeed a tailless Lesser Ape (India's only ape family, Hylobatidae), its Indian distribution is restricted exclusively to the southern bank of the Brahmaputra-Dibang river system across the seven northeastern states. It does not occur north of the Brahmaputra between the Sankosh and Manas rivers.

Row 2 is incorrectly matched. Gee's Golden Langur (Trachypithecus geei) is a leaf-eating Colobine monkey, but its global range is strictly confined to a small quadrate north of the Brahmaputra River—bounded by the Brahmaputra in the south, the Sankosh River in the west, the Manas River in the east, and the Black Mountains of Bhutan in the north (including Chakrashila Wildlife Sanctuary and Manas Biosphere Reserve).

Row 3 is correctly matched. The Grey Slender Loris (Loris lydekkerianus) is a small, nocturnal, arboreal strepsirrhine (prosimian) primate that feeds predominantly on ants, termites, and beetles in acacia thorn scrub, Euphorbia scrub, and dry deciduous forests of Southern India. India's first Slender Loris Sanctuary was notified across the Kadavur reserve forests in Karur and Dindigul districts of Tamil Nadu.

ref: Primates of Northeast India (Zoological Survey of India); Tamil Nadu Government Notification on Kadavur Slender Loris Sanctuary

stem: With reference to the ecological impact of the invasive alien shrub Lantana camara in Indian Tiger Reserves, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: High-density proliferation of Lantana camara in moist and dry deciduous forests paradoxically reduces the carrying capacity for apex carnivores like the Tiger, despite substantially increasing the total understory plant biomass.

Statement-II: Lantana camara suppresses native palatable grasses through allelopathic root exudates and dense canopy shading, while its leaves and unripe berries contain pentacyclic triterpenoids (lantadenes) that cause severe hepatotoxicity and photosensitization in mammalian herbivores.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Lantana camara degrades wild ungulate prey bases in Indian Tiger Reserves (such as Bandipur, Mudumalai, Corbett, and Satpura) by replacing nutritious native C4 grasses with unpalatable, hepatotoxic thorny thickets. Because apex predator density is directly governed by wild herbivore biomass, Lantana invasion lowers the trophic carrying capacity for tigers and leopards.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Extensive field studies across Indian Tiger Reserves (e.g., Mudumalai, Bandipur, Nagarahole, Rajaji, and Satpura) demonstrate that dense Lantana camara invasion transforms open grassy woodlands into impenetrable woody thickets. Although total understory woody biomass rises, the populations of principal wild prey species (such as Chital, Sambar, and Gaur) decline, which directly undermines the habitat's carrying capacity for apex carnivores.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Lantana camara releases phenolic allelochemicals into the soil that inhibit seed germination and growth of native understory herbs and palatable C4 grasses, while its dense overarching architecture blocks sunlight from reaching the forest floor. Furthermore, its foliage and unripe fruits contain pentacyclic triterpenoid acids (lantadene A and B) that induce cholestasis, liver damage (hepatotoxicity), and photosensitization in grazing ruminants, rendering the increased plant biomass unusable as forage for wild ungulates.

ref: All India Tiger Estimation (Status of Tigers, Co-predators and Prey in India) Reports, NTCA-WII

stem: With reference to the ecological impacts of Prosopis juliflora (locally known as Gando Baval or Seemai Karuvelam) in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It is a shallow-rooted obligate halophyte whose dense canopy reduces surface evaporation and progressively raises the local water table in arid aquifers.

2. Domestic livestock feeding on its protein-rich pods accelerate its invasion because passage through the ruminant digestive tract scarifies the hard seed coat and deposits viable seeds in nutrient-rich dung.

3. Beyond encroaching upon the Banni grasslands of Kutch, it has invaded the wetlands of Keoladeo National Park and the coral islands of the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, where its leaf litter releases allelopathic compounds that suppress native understory flora.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Prosopis juliflora is a deep-rooted phreatophyte that depletes groundwater, releases allelopathic phenolics (such as L-tryptophan and syringin), and relies on endozoochorous seed scarification via livestock digestion to colonize arid grasslands, wetlands, and coastal islands.

exp.why: Prosopis juliflora is not a shallow-rooted plant that raises the water table; rather, it is an aggressive, deep-rooted phreatophyte whose taproots can penetrate 30 to 50 metres (and even deeper) to tap directly into subterranean aquifers. By transpiring massive volumes of groundwater year-round, it severely lowers local water tables and desiccates soil moisture profiles in arid and semi-arid landscapes.

The sweet, carbohydrate- and protein-rich pods of Prosopis juliflora are readily consumed by cattle, buffaloes, sheep, and goats (such as the Maldhari livestock in the Banni grasslands). Because the seeds possess an impermeable, hard seed coat, passage through the acidic and enzymatic environment of the ruminant digestive tract mechanically and chemically scarifies the testa, breaking dormancy and depositing germinating seeds directly into moisture-retaining, nutrient-rich dung pats (endozoochory).

Originally introduced during the colonial and post-independence periods to combat desertification and fuelwood scarcity, Prosopis juliflora has degraded prime habitats across India, including the Banni grasslands of Kutch, the nesting wetlands of Keoladeo National Park (Bharatpur), and the coral reef islands (such as Kurusadai and Hare Island) in the Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve. Its foliage and roots exude water-soluble allelopathic phenolic alkaloids that inhibit the germination and growth of native palatable grasses and herbs.

ref: ENVIS Centre on Floral Diversity; Wildlife Institute of India (WII) Invasive Species Reports; Madras High Court & Supreme Court Directives on Seemai Karuvelam

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ecological impact of Water Hyacinth (Pontederia crassipes) in Indian freshwater ecosystems:
items: Statement-I: Dense surface mats of Water Hyacinth in Indian lentic wetlands cause mass mortality of native gill-breathing fish primarily by secreting neurotoxic alkaloids directly into the water column.

Statement-II: Extensive floating mats of Water Hyacinth block sunlight penetration to submerged autotrophs, physically impede atmospheric oxygen diffusion across the air-water interface, and sharply elevate Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) through microbial decomposition of senescent plant biomass.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Water Hyacinth (Pontederia crassipes / Eichhornia crassipes) causes fish kills not through chemical neurotoxins, but via physical and biochemical hypoxia resulting from surface shading, blocked air-water gas exchange, and high Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) during detritus decay.

exp.why: Water Hyacinth does not kill native gill-breathing fish by secreting neurotoxic alkaloids into the water column. The mass mortality of aquatic fauna in infested wetlands (such as Deepor Beel, Harike, Vembanad, and the floodplain beels of Kaziranga) is driven by severe dissolved oxygen depletion (hypoxia and anoxia) rather than direct phytotoxin poisoning.

Propagating rapidly via vegetative stolons, Water Hyacinth forms interlocking floating mats across lentic waterbodies. These mats cut off photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) to submerged macrophytes and phytoplankton (halting underwater photosynthetic oxygen production), seal the water surface against atmospheric oxygen diffusion, and generate massive quantities of dead organic litter whose aerobic microbial decomposition consumes dissolved oxygen, driving up Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD).

ref: Wetlands International South Asia; NCERT Class XII Biology Ch. 13 & 15; National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Eco-systems (NPCA)

stem: With reference to invasive alien plant species threatening Indian Protected Areas and their ecological management, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Clear-felling the trunks of Senna spectabilis at ground level in the Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve permanently eradicates the tree without requiring debarking or root extraction, as the species lacks dormant subterranean vegetative buds.
2. Mikania micrantha is a xerophytic thorny shrub that colonizes hyper-arid desert dunes in western Rajasthan because its seeds require prolonged drought to break dormancy.

3. Parthenium hysterophorus enhances the germination of native palatable grasses in Indian wildlife sanctuaries by fixing atmospheric nitrogen through symbiotic root nodules while remaining non-allergenic to mammalian herbivores.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Effective management of invasive flora requires species-specific biological interventions: Senna spectabilis coppices vigorously if cut without collar-debarking or uprooting, Mikania micrantha is a humid-zone climbing vine smothering moist forests and grasslands, and Parthenium hysterophorus is a non-leguminous weed that suppresses native flora via allelopathic sesquiterpene lactones.

exp.why: Simply felling Senna spectabilis trunks at stump level is counterproductive because the tree possesses extraordinary coppicing vigour from dormant epicormic and root-collar buds. When cut without stripping the bark down to the root collar (girdling/debarking to starve the roots of phloem photosynthates) or mechanically uprooting sapling rootstocks, a single felled trunk regenerates into a dense multi-stemmed thicket, worsening the invasion across Wayanad, Mudumalai, Bandipur, and Sathyamangalam Tiger Reserves.

Mikania micrantha (commonly called the 'mile-a-minute' weed) is not a xerophytic desert shrub; it is a fast-growing perennial climbing vine native to the humid Neotropics. In India, it aggressively invades high-rainfall, moist ecosystems such as the alluvial grasslands and sal forests of Kaziranga, Manas, the Terai-Duar belt, and moist deciduous openings in the Western Ghats, where it smothers canopy trees and tall grasses by blocking sunlight.

Parthenium hysterophorus (Congress grass) belongs to the family Asteraceae, lacks Rhizobium-bearing root nodules, and does not fix atmospheric nitrogen. Instead, it releases potent allelopathic sesquiterpene lactones (principally parthenin) and phenolic acids into the soil that inhibit the germination and root elongation of native grasses, while causing severe contact dermatitis, respiratory allergies, and hepatic toxicity in livestock and wild ungulates.

ref: Kerala Forest Research Institute (KFRI) Senna Management Protocols; Status of Tigers, Co-predators and Prey in India (NTCA-WII Report)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding invasive alien fauna introduced into Indian freshwater ecosystems:
items: 1. The African Catfish (Clarias gariepinus), despite being prohibited for aquaculture in India, persists in degraded and hypoxic waterbodies due to its accessory air-breathing organs and preys voraciously on native carps and amphibians.

2. The Mosquitofish (Gambusia affinis), introduced into Indian freshwater bodies for biological vector control, possesses a specialized mouthpart morphology that restricts its diet to surface-dwelling dipteran larvae, thereby sparing submerged native fish roe and amphibian tadpoles from predation.

3. The Suckermouth Sailfin Catfish (Pterygoplichthys spp.) and the Red-Eared Slider Turtle (Trachemys scripta elegans) have entered Indian river systems primarily through the ornamental aquarium and pet trade, where the former destabilizes riverbanks through nesting burrows and the latter outcompetes native freshwater turtles for basking sites.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Invasive freshwater fauna in India originate from clandestine aquaculture (Clarias gariepinus), misguided biological vector control (Gambusia affinis, a generalist predator of native fish eggs and tadpoles), and the ornamental pet trade (Pterygoplichthys spp. and Trachemys scripta elegans).

exp.why: Although the Ministry of Agriculture and the National Green Tribunal banned the breeding and culture of the African Catfish (Clarias gariepinus), it remains widespread in Indian wetlands and rivers. Equipped with arborescent suprabranchial accessory breathing organs, it can survive in oxygen-depleted waters and crawl across wet land between ponds, decimating native cyprinids, amphibians, and even waterfowl chicks.

Gambusia affinis (Mosquitofish) is not a specialist feeder restricted to mosquito larvae. Its upturned mouth adapts it to surface feeding, but it is a highly aggressive, opportunistic omnivore/predator that consumes zooplankton, aquatic insects, the eggs and fry of native larvivorous fishes (such as Aplocheilus and Puntius species), and endemic amphibian tadpoles. Due to this severe ecological damage, the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) and ZSI classify Gambusia affinis as an invasive alien species in India.

Both the armour-plated Suckermouth Sailfin Catfish (Pterygoplichthys pardalis / P. disjunctivus) and the Red-Eared Slider Turtle (Trachemys scripta elegans) were introduced via the unregulated aquarium and exotic pet trade. Male Pterygoplichthys excavate deep horizontal spawning tunnels into earthen embankments, causing riverbank collapse and siltation, while released Red-Eared Sliders mature rapidly, monopolize thermal basking sites, and transmit parasites to native Indian roofed and flapshell turtles.

ref: Zoological Survey of India (ZSI) & National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) Invasive Alien Species Lists; NGT Orders on Clarias gariepinus

stem: In the context of India's Project Cheetah, the intercontinental translocation of Southern African cheetahs (Acinonyx jubatus jubatus) from Namibia and South Africa across the equator into Central Indian landscapes such as Kuno National Park and Gandhi Sagar Wildlife Sanctuary has presented a distinct physiological challenge during the Indian summer and monsoon months. Which one of the following best explains the primary biological mechanism behind this challenge?

opts.A: Southern African cheetahs lack the semi-retractable claws and digital pads required to gain traction on the basaltic vertisols and alluvial soils of the Vindhyan range during wet conditions.
opts.B: Unlike Asiatic felids, Southern African cheetahs are obligate nocturnal hunters whose dark malar facial stripes impair visual acuity under the diffused cloud cover of the Indian monsoon.
opts.C: Entrained to Southern Hemisphere circannual photoperiod rhythms, translocated cheetahs may develop a dense winter coat coinciding with the hot, humid Indian summer and monsoon, predisposing their skin to moisture retention, ectoparasitic dermatitis, and fly-strike myiasis.
opts.D: Southern African cheetahs possess hyper-enlarged nasal cavities that cannot filter high atmospheric humidity, resulting in acute pulmonary edema whenever ambient relative humidity exceeds seventy percent.

core: Trans-hemispheric wildlife translocation across the equator disrupts photoperiod-driven circannual rhythms; Southern African cheetahs programmed to grow winter coats during June–August experience severe thermal and dermatological stress when those months correspond to the hot, humid Indian summer and southwest monsoon.

exp.why: Option C is correct: In the Southern Hemisphere (Namibia and South Africa), June to August is winter, and cheetahs' endogenous circannual rhythms (regulated by photoperiod/day-length cues via melatonin signalling) trigger the growth of a thick winter coat during these months. When translocated across the equator to the Northern Hemisphere in Central India (Kuno and Gandhi Sagar), June to September corresponds to extreme pre-monsoon heat followed by the warm, high-humidity southwest monsoon. Developing a dense winter coat during humid Indian rains traps moisture and sweat against the skin, causing maceration, itchiness (leading to self-inflicted scratch wounds on trees), bacterial dermatitis, maggot infestation (fly-strike myiasis), and fatal septicemia. Option A is incorrect because all cheetahs possess semi-retractable claws and hard, ridged digital pads that function like traction cleats across varied savanna and woodland soils. Option B is incorrect because cheetahs are predominantly diurnal/crepuscular cursorial hunters (to avoid nocturnal kleptoparasitism by lions and leopards), and their dark malar 'tear stripes' absorb solar glare during daylight chases. Option D is incorrect because their enlarged nasal passages and bronchioles are evolutionary adaptations for high oxygen intake during sprints and do not cause humidity-induced pulmonary edema.

ref: Action Plan for Introduction of Cheetah in India (WII-NTCA-MoEFCC); Project Cheetah Annual Progress Reports (2023–2025)

stem: With reference to the ecology, distribution, and statutory protection of wild equids in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Indian Wild Ass (Equus hemionus khur) is adapted to the saline mudflats of the Little Rann of Kutch, where its populations congregate during the monsoon on elevated, salt-free plateaus locally known as 'bets' that support halophytic grasses and sedges.
2. The Tibetan Wild Ass or Kiang (Equus kiang), which is the largest of all living wild asses, inhabits the high-altitude cold desert steppes and alpine meadows of Ladakh and northern Sikkim.

3. While the Indian Wild Ass is accorded the highest statutory protection under Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, the Tibetan Wild Ass is placed under Schedule V as a vermin species to permit regulated culling against pasture competition in border districts.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India hosts two native wild equid taxa—the Indian Wild Ass (Khur) in the saline flats and 'bets' of the Little Rann of Kutch and adjacent Gujarat landscapes, and the Tibetan Wild Ass (Kiang) in the Trans-Himalayan steppes of Ladakh and Sikkim—both of which enjoy the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972.

exp.why: The Indian Wild Ass or Khur (Equus hemionus khur) has its stronghold in the Indian Wild Ass Sanctuary in the Little Rann of Kutch (and dispersing corridors towards the Greater Rann and Nalsarovar). When the flat saline mudflats ('pats') are inundated during the southwest monsoon by marine ingress and seasonal rivers (such as the Banas, Saraswati, and Rupen), the Khur takes refuge and breeds on slightly elevated, low-salinity islands called 'bets' covered with xerophytic and halophytic grasses.

The Tibetan Wild Ass or Kiang (Equus kiang) is the largest wild ass species in the world. Adapted to extreme cold and hypoxia at elevations between 4,000 and 5,500 metres, it occurs in the Trans-Himalayan cold desert steppes of Changthang in Ladakh as well as the cold alpine plateaus of northern Sikkim (such as Tso Lhamo and Lashar Valley).

Both the Indian Wild Ass (Equus hemionus khur) and the Tibetan Wild Ass (Equus kiang) are listed under Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, conferring the highest level of legal protection against hunting. Furthermore, the Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 rationalized the Act into only four schedules (Schedules I, II, III, and IV), completely abolishing the erstwhile Schedule V (Vermin); the Central Government now notifies vermin solely by notification under Section 62, and the Kiang has never been declared vermin.

ref: Wild Life (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (Schedule I); IUCN Equid Specialist Group; WII Trans-Himalayan & Kutch Biodiversity Assessments

stem: Consider the following flagship Himalayan ungulates along with their primary protected-area strongholds in India:
items: 1. Hangul (Dachigam National Park)
2. Kashmir Markhor (Kajinag National Park)
3. Mishmi Takin (Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary)
4. White-bellied Musk Deer (Askot Wildlife Sanctuary)
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct spatial sequence of the above strongholds as one proceeds from West to East across the Indian Himalayan Region?
core: Specialized Himalayan ungulates occupy distinct longitudinal and altitudinal niches from the western Pir Panjal and Zabarwan ranges in Jammu and Kashmir through the Kumaon Himalayas of Uttarakhand to the Mishmi Hills of eastern Arunachal Pradesh. Mapping flagship species to their core strongholds tests fine-scale biogeographical literacy across the Western, Central, and Eastern Himalayas.

exp.why: The Hangul or Kashmir Stag (Cervus hanglu hanglu), a Critically Endangered subspecies of the Central Asian Red Deer and the UT animal of Jammu and Kashmir, has its only viable wild population in Dachigam National Park (~75.0 degrees E longitude) in the Zabarwan Range northeast of Srinagar, placing it second from the west.

The Kashmir Markhor (Capra falconeri cashmiriensis), the world's largest wild goat characterized by corkscrew-shaped horns, inhabits precipitous cliffs of the western Pir Panjal and Jhelum valley. Its core Indian stronghold is Kajinag National Park (~74.1 degrees E longitude) in Baramulla district near the Line of Control, making it the westernmost stronghold among the four.

The Mishmi Takin (Budorcas taxicolor taxicolor), a stocky goat-antelope adapted to dense bamboo and rhododendron thickets, is found in the easternmost Mishmi Hills of Arunachal Pradesh inside Dibang Wildlife Sanctuary and the Dihang-Dibang Biosphere Reserve (~95.8 degrees E longitude), placing it farthest east.

The Himalayan White-bellied Musk Deer (Moschus leucogaster), a solitary tragulid-like ungulate lacking antlers and possessing a caudal musk gland in males, inhabits subalpine birch-rhododendron zones (2,500-4,300 m) in Askot Wildlife Sanctuary (~80.3 degrees E longitude) in Pithoragarh district of eastern Uttarakhand, placing it third from the west between Dachigam and Dibang.

ref: Wildlife Institute of India (WII) ENVIS Ungulate Profiles; Rodgers & Panwar Biogeographic Classification of India

stem: With reference to the taxonomy, morphology, and biogeographical distribution of the Red Panda in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Despite both possessing a modified radial sesamoid bone functioning as a 'false thumb' to grasp bamboo stems, the Red Panda and the Giant Panda belong to different mammalian families and represent an example of convergent evolution.

2. India naturally hosts both the Himalayan Red Panda (Ailurus fulgens) and the Chinese Red Panda (Ailurus styani), with the Siang River in Arunachal Pradesh acting as the biogeographical boundary separating the two species.

3. In India, its natural habitat comprises montane temperate broadleaf and mixed coniferous forests with a dense bamboo understory across protected areas such as Singalila, Neora Valley, Khangchendzonga, and Namdapha National Parks.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Red Panda is the sole living representative of the family Ailuridae (superfamily Musteloidea) and is phylogenetically distant from the Giant Panda (family Ursidae), sharing its 'false thumb' only through convergent adaptation to a bamboo-dominated diet. Within India, the Siang River in Arunachal Pradesh forms a major Pleistocene riverine barrier separating the Himalayan Red Panda (west of Siang) from the Chinese/Styan's Red Panda (east of Siang).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Both the Red Panda and the Giant Panda possess an enlarged radial sesamoid wrist bone ('false thumb') for manipulating bamboo culms. However, genomic and morphological evidence confirms that the Giant Panda is a true bear (family Ursidae), whereas the Red Panda belongs to its own distinct family Ailuridae closely allied to mustelids and procyonids, making the false thumb a textbook case of convergent evolution.

Statement 2 is correct. Phylogeographic studies by the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI) established that India is home to both recognized species of Red Panda: the Himalayan Red Panda (Ailurus fulgens) distributed across Darjeeling-Kalimpong, Sikkim, and western/central Arunachal Pradesh, and the Chinese Red Panda (Ailurus styani) occurring east of the Siang River in eastern Arunachal Pradesh.

Statement 3 is correct. The Red Panda is an arboreal habitat specialist of the Eastern Himalayas (typically 2,200-4,000 m altitude), requiring mature temperate broadleaf-conifer forests with hollow trees for maternity dens and a dense understory of ringal bamboo (Thamnocalamus and Yushania species) in parks such as Singalila and Neora Valley (West Bengal), Khangchendzonga (Sikkim), and Namdapha/Mouling (Arunachal Pradesh).

ref: Zoological Survey of India (ZSI) Red Panda Phylogeography Report; IUCN Red List; Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (Schedule I)

stem: With reference to the anatomical adaptations and geographical distribution of Pangolins in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the keratinous horns of rhinoceroses, the overlapping defensive scales of pangolins are dermal plates composed of calcified bone and chitin fused to the underlying vertebrae.

2. Being completely toothless, pangolins capture ants and termites using an elongated sticky tongue anchored near the pelvis and grind their prey inside a muscular, gizzard-like stomach containing keratinous spines and ingested pebbles.

3. While the Indian Pangolin (Manis crassicaudata) occurs widely across peninsular India, the distribution of the Chinese Pangolin (Manis pentadactyla) in India is restricted to the Himalayan foothills and the Northeastern states.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Pangolins (order Pholidota) are the only mammals wholly covered in overlapping epidermal scales made of keratin, not bone or chitin. Their specialized myrmecophagous anatomy includes complete edentulism, a ribcage-to-pelvis-anchored tongue, and a gastrolith-assisted muscular pyloric stomach, with two species occupying distinct yet partially overlapping ranges in India.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Like rhinoceros horns and human fingernails, pangolin scales are epidermal derivatives composed entirely of keratin (specifically alpha- and beta-keratin), not calcified bone (which forms armadillo osteoderms) or chitin (which forms arthropod exoskeletons). Furthermore, the scales are attached to the dermis/epidermis and are never fused to the vertebrae, enabling the animal to curl into an impenetrable ball when threatened.

Statement 2 is correct. Pangolins are obligate myrmecophages that lack teeth and the ability to chew. Their remarkably long, sticky tongue is anchored to the xiphisternum near the pelvis, and swallowed ants and termites are mechanically crushed inside a thick-walled, muscular pyloric stomach lined with keratinous spines and aided by intentionally ingested small stones (gastroliths).

Statement 3 is correct. India is home to two of the eight extant pangolin species: the Endangered Indian Pangolin (Manis crassicaudata), distributed across peninsular India, central plains, and the arid northwest, and the Critically Endangered Chinese Pangolin (Manis pentadactyla), confined within India to the eastern Himalayan foothills, Bihar/Assam plains, and the Northeastern states. Both enjoy the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.

ref: ZSI Handbook on Indian Mammals; CITES Appendix I; Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (Schedule I)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the reproductive ecology and conservation of the Olive Ridley Sea Turtle (Lepidochelys olivacea) along the eastern coast of India:
items: Statement-I: Persistently warmer beach sand temperatures caused by climate change and marine heatwaves on Odisha's mass-nesting (Arribada) beaches at Gahirmatha, Rushikulya, and the Devi river mouth threaten the long-term demographic stability of Olive Ridley Sea Turtle populations by skewing hatchling sex ratios heavily toward females.

Statement-II: To reduce incidental mortality of adult breeding turtles congregating in nearshore coastal waters, mechanized fishing trawlers operating off the Odisha coast are mandated to fit Turtle Excluder Devices (TEDs) in their trawl nets.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Marine turtles lack sex chromosomes (XX/XY) and instead exhibit Temperature-Dependent Sex Determination (TSD), wherein incubation temperatures above the pivotal threshold (~29.5-30 degrees C) upregulate aromatase enzyme activity to produce females, while cooler temperatures produce males. While TEDs mitigate adult bycatch mortality in nearshore waters, they do not explain the embryonic thermal physiology governing hatchling sex ratios in beach nests.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Olive Ridley Sea Turtles exhibit Temperature-Dependent Sex Determination (TSD Type Ia) during the middle third (thermosensitive period) of egg incubation in beach sand. Incubation temperatures below ~28 degrees C yield predominantly males, whereas temperatures above ~30-31 degrees C yield almost exclusively females; hence rising sand temperatures on Odisha's rookeries risk feminizing hatchling cohorts.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. A Turtle Excluder Device (TED) is a specialized metal grid fitted into the neck of a shrimp/fish trawl net that allows small target catch to pass into the cod-end while directing air-breathing sea turtles out through an escape hatch to prevent drowning. Statement-I is explained by thermal regulation of gonadal aromatase expression during embryonic incubation, not by trawler bycatch mitigation.

ref: WII Sea Turtle Research Programme; Orissa Marine Fishing Regulation Act; IUCN Marine Turtle Specialist Group

stem: Which one of the following statements best describes the ecological role of the Dugong (Dugong dugon) as an 'ecosystem engineer' in Indian coastal waters?

opts.A: As India's only strictly herbivorous marine mammal, its rotational 'cultivation grazing' uproots older, fiber-rich seagrass shoots in shallow bays such as Palk Bay and the Gulf of Mannar, aerating benthic sediments and stimulating the rapid regrowth of nitrogen-rich pioneer seagrass species that enhance 'blue carbon' sequestration.
opts.B: As an apex carnivorous cetacean in estuarine mangrove creeks, it regulates benthic crustacean and molluscan populations, preventing overgrazing of mangrove pneumatophores along the Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika coasts.
opts.C: It performs deep-diving vertical migrations to aphotic hydrothermal vents along the Central Indian Ridge, transporting chemosynthetic nutrients to surface coral reef ecosystems in Lakshadweep.
opts.D: It is an amphibious freshwater sirenean endemic to coastal oxbow lakes and brackish lagoons such as Chilika and Pulicat, where it controls invasive water hyacinth blooms.

core: The Dugong (order Sirenia) is India's sole strictly herbivorous marine mammal, restricted to shallow coastal seagrass beds in the Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kutch, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Through 'cultivation grazing', dugongs disturb the sediment, recycle nutrients, and promote fast-growing, high-nitrogen, low-fiber pioneer seagrass genera (such as Halophila and Halodule), maintaining the productivity and carbon-trapping capacity of coastal blue carbon meadows.

exp.why: Option A is correct because the Dugong (Sea Cow) is an obligate marine herbivore (order Sirenia, not Cetacea) whose foraging behaviour—often termed 'cultivation grazing'—uproots whole seagrass plants (Halophila, Cymodocea, Halodule, Syringodium) along shallow photic seafloors in Palk Bay (where India's first Dugong Conservation Reserve was notified in Tamil Nadu), the Gulf of Mannar, the Gulf of Kutch, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. This grazing prevents meadow senescence, aerates anaerobic sediments, and stimulates rapid regrowth of nutrient-dense pioneer seagrasses, strengthening coastal blue carbon sinks. Option B is incorrect because dugongs are neither cetaceans nor carnivores and do not inhabit the Sundarbans. Option C is incorrect because dugongs are restricted to shallow coastal photic zones (<10-15 m) where photosynthetic seagrasses grow. Option D is incorrect because dugongs are strictly marine (unlike some manatees) and do not inhabit Chilika or Pulicat to feed on freshwater weeds.

ref: CAMPA-Dugong Recovery Programme (WII); Tamil Nadu Palk Bay Dugong Conservation Reserve Notification

stem: With reference to the biology of Critically Endangered vultures in India and the pharmacology of veterinary non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Among the veterinary NSAIDs administered to cattle in India, Diclofenac is the sole compound that causes uric acid crystallization and visceral gout in Gyps vultures, whereas Aceclofenac, Ketoprofen, and Nimesulide are physiologically non-toxic to scavenging raptors.

2. Both Meloxicam and Tolfenamic acid have been banned for veterinary use by the Union Government after toxicology trials revealed that they bioaccumulate in livestock tissues and induce acute renal failure in vultures.

3. While the Indian Vulture (Gyps indicus) breeds exclusively in colonies on tall trees in riverine plains, the White-rumped Vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and Slender-billed Vulture (Gyps tenuirostris) are obligate cliff-nesters restricted to rocky crags and gorges.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Multiple veterinary NSAIDs—specifically Diclofenac, Aceclofenac (a prodrug that metabolizes into Diclofenac inside cattle), Ketoprofen, and Nimesulide—inhibit renal uric acid excretion in Gyps vultures, causing hyperuricemia, visceral gout, and death within days of scavenging a treated carcass. Conversely, Meloxicam and Tolfenamic acid are verified vulture-safe alternatives promoted under India's Action Plan for Vulture Conservation (APVC).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Diclofenac is not the only nephrotoxic NSAID for vultures. Aceclofenac is rapidly metabolized into Diclofenac inside treated cattle, and both Ketoprofen and Nimesulide have been clinically proven to cause identical renal tubular damage, hyperuricemia, and fatal visceral gout in Gyps vultures. Consequently, the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has banned the veterinary manufacture, sale, and distribution of Diclofenac, Aceclofenac, Ketoprofen, and Nimesulide under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Meloxicam and Tolfenamic acid are the two officially validated 'vulture-safe' veterinary NSAIDs in India. Safety trials conducted by the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) and the Indian Veterinary Research Institute (IVRI) confirmed that vultures rapidly eliminate Meloxicam and Tolfenamic acid without suffering renal toxicity, and both drugs are actively promoted as safe substitutes.

Statement 3 is incorrect because it swaps the nesting ecology of the species. The Indian Vulture or Long-billed Vulture (Gyps indicus) is predominantly a cliff-nesting species that breeds on rocky crags, escarpments, and steep gorges across central and peninsular India, whereas the White-rumped Vulture (Gyps bengalensis) and Slender-billed Vulture (Gyps tenuirostris) are tree-nesting species that build stick nests in tall trees.

ref: Action Plan for Vulture Conservation (APVC) 2020-2025 (MoEFCC); Drugs and Cosmetics Act Section 26A Notifications on Veterinary NSAIDs

stem: With reference to the herpetofauna of the Western Ghats, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Purple Frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) : Arboreal canopy dweller that constructs suspended foam nests over forest pools
2. Malabar Gliding Frog (Rhacophorus malabaricus) : Fossorial amphibian that spends almost the entire year underground and emerges briefly during pre-monsoon showers
3. Western Ghats King Cobra (Ophiophagus kaalinga) : Primarily ophiophagous snake in which the female constructs an elevated leaf-litter mound nest
4. Cochin Forest Cane Turtle (Vijayachelys silvatica) : Estuarine chelonian that undertakes synchronized mass nesting along sandy coastal beaches
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Western Ghats harbour highly specialized endemic herpetofauna partitioned across subterranean, terrestrial leaf-litter, and arboreal niches. Distinguishing the fossorial life history of the Purple Frog from the arboreal foam-nesting strategy of rhacophorid tree frogs, alongside the unique nest-building behaviour of the King Cobra, is essential for ecological classification.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched due to an ecological swap with the Malabar Gliding Frog. The Purple Frog (Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis) is an ancient, evolutionarily distinct fossorial (burrowing) amphibian that spends nearly the entire year underground feeding on subterranean termites and emerges only for a few days during pre-monsoon showers to breed in seasonal hill streams.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The Malabar Gliding Frog (Rhacophorus malabaricus) is an arboreal canopy species equipped with extensively webbed feet that allow it to parachuting-glide between trees; it constructs foam nests suspended on vegetation overhanging stagnant water bodies.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. The King Cobra (including the Western Ghats lineage Ophiophagus kaalinga) is primarily ophiophagous (feeding on other snakes such as rat snakes and pit vipers) and is the only snake group in the world where the female actively gathers leaf litter with her body coils to construct an above-ground, multi-chambered mound nest and guards the clutch.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The Cochin Forest Cane Turtle (Vijayachelys silvatica) is a small, cryptic terrestrial turtle strictly endemic to the moist leaf litter of dense evergreen and semi-evergreen forests in the Western Ghats; it has no association with estuarine habitats or coastal mass nesting (arribada).

ref: IUCN Red List Profiles of Western Ghats Herpetofauna; BNHS Book of Indian Reptiles and Amphibians

stem: With reference to the ecology and conservation of the Pygmy Hog (Porcula salvania), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the Pygmy Hog and the Hispid Hare (Caprolagus hispidus) serve as sympatric indicator species of undisturbed, early-successional tall wet alluvial grasslands in the Himalayan foothill Bhabar-Terai belt.
2. Unlike most other wild suids that build nests only prior to farrowing, both male and female Pygmy Hogs construct and utilize roofed grass nests throughout the year.

3. Complete and permanent suppression of fire to allow tall Terai grasslands to naturally succeed into closed-canopy Sal (Shorea robusta) woodland is essential for expanding the natural habitat of the Pygmy Hog.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Pygmy Hog (Porcula salvania) and Hispid Hare (Caprolagus hispidus) are obligate specialists of early-successional tall wet alluvial grasslands (Narenga-Saccharum communities) in Assam's Manas and Orang landscapes. Sustaining their habitat requires preventing both destructive late-dry-season sweeping fires and complete fire exclusion, as the latter drives ecological succession into closed woodland.

exp.why: Both the Pygmy Hog (the world's smallest and rarest wild pig) and the Hispid Hare co-occur in the early-successional tall wet alluvial grasslands of the Bhabar-Terai tract (principally Manas and Orang National Parks) and act as sensitive bio-indicators of intact wet grassland ecosystems.

A distinctive behavioral trait of the Pygmy Hog among Suidae is that both sexes construct and use dome-shaped, roofed thatch nests lined with cut grass throughout the year—not merely for farrowing—to protect themselves against nocturnal chill, heat, and predators.

Tall wet alluvial grasslands are seral (early-successional) ecosystems maintained by seasonal flooding and periodic disturbance. Complete exclusion of fire accelerates woody encroachment and natural ecological succession into closed-canopy Sal (Shorea robusta) or bombax woodland, which renders the habitat completely unsuitable for the obligate grassland-dwelling Pygmy Hog. Instead, scientific conservation relies on controlled, early-season patch burning as an alternative to destructive late-dry-season fires.

ref: Pygmy Hog Conservation Programme (PHCP) Reports; MoEFCC Species Recovery Programme

stem: With reference to the wild canids and hyaenids native to India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Indian Grey Wolf (Canis lupus pallipes) is an obligate closed-canopy forest predator whose primary distribution in India is confined to the wet evergreen forests of the Northeast and the Western Ghats.
2. The Dhole or Asiatic Wild Dog (Cuon alpinus) is a solitary, strictly nocturnal scavenger adapted primarily for crushing large bones rather than hunting live ungulates.
3. Under the amended Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, the Striped Hyena (Hyaena hyaena) is permanently classified as a vermin species across peninsular India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's large guild of non-felid carnivores exhibits sharp ecological and morphological niche partitioning: the Indian Grey Wolf dominates semi-arid open grasslands and scrublands, the Dhole is a diurnal social pack hunter in wooded landscapes, and the Striped Hyena is a nocturnal bone-crushing scavenger accorded top statutory protection under Schedule I.

exp.why: The Indian Grey Wolf (Canis lupus pallipes) avoids dense, wet evergreen closed-canopy forests. Instead, it is the apex predator of India's semi-arid open plains, dry grasslands, thorn scrublands, and agro-pastoral landscapes across peninsular and western India (such as Velavadar Blackbuck National Park in Gujarat and Bankapura Wolf Sanctuary in Karnataka).

This statement swaps the ecology of the Dhole with that of the Striped Hyena. The Dhole (Cuon alpinus) is a highly social, predominantly diurnal cursorial pack hunter and hypercarnivore that actively pursues live forest ungulates. It is the Striped Hyena (Hyaena hyaena) that is predominantly nocturnal, forages solitarily, and possesses specialized premolars and jaw musculature for crushing heavy bones.

Under the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, the earlier permanent Vermin Schedule (old Schedule V) was abolished, and vermin can only be temporarily notified by the Central Government under Section 62 for specific areas and durations. Moreover, the Striped Hyena is strictly protected under Schedule I of the Act due to its critical ecological role in carcass disposal.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022; Prater's Book of Indian Animals

stem: With reference to the bear species native to India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Among the four bear species found in India, the Sloth Bear (Melursus ursinus) is the only myrmecophagous specialist that lacks two upper central incisors to form a suction gap and routinely carries its young cubs on its back.

2. To survive acute summer water and food scarcity across the rocky deciduous scrublands of the Deccan Plateau, the Sloth Bear undergoes mandatory physiological hibernation for up to four months every year.

3. While the Himalayan Brown Bear (Ursus arctos isabellinus) inhabits high-altitude alpine meadows above the tree line in the Western and Northwestern Himalayas, the Malayan Sun Bear (Helarctos malayanus) in India is restricted to the forested hill tracts of the Northeast.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India supports four bear species partitioned by altitude and feeding morphology: the non-hibernating, termite-eating Sloth Bear across peninsular and lowland forests; the hibernating Himalayan Brown Bear in alpine pastures; the Asiatic Black Bear in mid-elevation Himalayan and northeastern forests; and the arboreal Sun Bear in the eastern borderlands of Northeast India.

exp.why: The Sloth Bear exhibits specialized morphological adaptations for myrmecophagy (feeding on termites and ants): a mobile snout, voluntarily closable nostrils, a concave palate, and the congenital absence of two upper central incisors, creating a permanent gap through which it sucks up insects like a vacuum. Furthermore, female Sloth Bears are unique among bears in routinely carrying their cubs on their backs for the first several months of life as a defense against predators like tigers and leopards.

Sloth Bears do not hibernate or estivate. Inhabiting warm tropical and subtropical dry and moist deciduous forests and boulder-strewn scrublands (such as Daroji in Karnataka and Jessore in Gujarat), they remain active throughout the year, shifting seasonally between termites and fruiting trees like Mahua, Jamun, and Ziziphus. True winter hibernation in India is exhibited by the Himalayan Brown Bear and high-altitude populations of the Asiatic Black Bear.

The Himalayan Brown Bear occupies sub-alpine scrub and alpine meadows above the tree line (3,000 to 5,000 metres) across Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand. Conversely, the Malayan Sun Bear—the world's smallest bear species—occurs within India exclusively in the tropical and subtropical evergreen forests of Northeast India bordering Myanmar (such as Namdapha, Dampa, and Fakim).

ref: IUCN Bear Specialist Group Profiles; Wildlife Institute of India (WII) National Bear Conservation Action Plan

stem: Consider the following biological taxa and specimens regulated under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022):
items: 1. Beddome's Cycad (Cycas beddomei), an endemic protected plant of the Eastern Ghats
2. Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps), a critically endangered native bird accorded the highest level of statutory protection
3. Blue-and-yellow Macaw (Ara ararauna), an exotic neotropical bird listed in the Appendices of CITES
4. Nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus), a native wild ungulate accorded the second tier of statutory protection
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct sequential arrangement of the above taxa according to their respective Schedules (from Schedule I to Schedule IV) under the currently enforced Act?
core: The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 rationalized the earlier six-schedule framework into exactly four Schedules: Schedule I (animal species with the highest protection), Schedule II (animal species with a lesser degree of protection), Schedule III (protected plant species, replacing the old Schedule VI), and Schedule IV (specimens listed in the Appendices of CITES).

exp.why: Under the rationalized four-schedule architecture introduced by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022, all specified Protected Plant Species (such as Beddome's Cycad, Neelakurinji, Pitcher Plant, and Red Vanda), which were previously placed in the old Schedule VI, are now consolidated under Schedule III.

The Great Indian Bustard (Ardeotis nigriceps) is placed in Schedule I, which covers native wild fauna accorded the highest degree of statutory protection and attracts the strictest penal provisions for hunting or trade.

To give statutory effect to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) under Chapter VB of the Act, the 2022 Amendment created a dedicated Schedule IV exclusively for specimens listed in the CITES Appendices, such as exotic Macaws, African Grey Parrots, and Red-eared Sliders.

The Nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus) is listed in Schedule II of the amended Act, which covers native wild animal species accorded the second tier of statutory protection. Ordering the four items progressively from Schedule I -> Schedule II -> Schedule III -> Schedule IV yields the sequence 2 - 4 - 1 - 3.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (Schedules I, II, III and IV)

stem: With reference to the Swamp Deer or Barasingha (Rucervus duvaucelii) found in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. All three extant subspecies of the Barasingha in India are obligate marsh-dwellers possessing widely splayed hooves and are restricted to the seasonal floodplains of the Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems.

2. Among the three subspecies, the Hard-ground Barasingha (Rucervus duvaucelii branderi) is the only one adapted to firm, dry open grassy meadows in central India and possesses compact, well-knit hooves.

3. In the upper Gangetic plains, natural populations of the Wetland Barasingha (Rucervus duvaucelii duvaucelii) inhabit the tall wet grasslands and seasonal marshes (taals) of the Dudhwa-Kishanpur landscape and Jhilmil Jheel Conservation Reserve.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: India's three extant subspecies of Barasingha illustrate adaptive morphological divergence between floodplain marshes and central Indian uplands: while the Northern (R. d. duvaucelii) and Eastern (R. d. ranjitsinhi) subspecies have splayed hooves for boggy riverine grasslands, the Central Indian Hard-ground Barasingha (R. d. branderi) evolved hard, well-knit hooves for dry meadows.

exp.why: This statement over-generalizes the traits of the floodplain subspecies to all three subspecies.
