It does not replace national laws; rather, it provides a framework that each Party must operationalize by adopting domestic legislation (such as Chapter VB of India's Wildlife Protection Act) to penalize illegal trade and authorize confiscation of specimens.

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article I(c) and I(e) of CITES, 'trade' encompasses four distinct activities: export, re-export, import, and 'introduction from the sea'. 'Introduction from the sea' means transportation into a State of specimens of any species included in Appendix I or II which were taken in the marine environment not under the jurisdiction of any State (i.e., the high seas / areas beyond national jurisdiction), requiring a prior certificate from the Management Authority of the State of introduction after a Non-Detriment Finding.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Article IX of CITES, each Party must designate one or more Management Authorities competent to grant permits or certificates on behalf of that Party, and one or more Scientific Authorities to provide independent scientific evaluations, including Non-Detriment Findings (NDFs), to ensure trade is not detrimental to the survival of the species.

ref: CITES Text Articles I, VIII & IX

stem: Consider the following pairs regarding the Appendices of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) and their respective regulatory rules:
items: 1. Appendix I : Includes 'look-alike' species not necessarily threatened with extinction today; international trade requires an Export Permit but no prior Import Permit under the Convention.

2. Appendix II : Includes species threatened with extinction; international commercial trade is generally prohibited and any permitted exceptional trade requires the prior grant of both an Import Permit and an Export Permit.

3. Appendix III : Includes species listed unilaterally at the request of a Party that already regulates them within its jurisdiction; export from that listing Party requires an Export Permit issued by its Management Authority.
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: CITES calibrates permit stringency across three Appendices: Appendix I (threatened with extinction) requires both a prior Import Permit and an Export Permit; Appendix II (potentially threatened or look-alike species) requires an Export Permit based on a Non-Detriment Finding without a mandatory CITES Import Permit; and Appendix III allows unilateral national listing where exports from the listing country require an Export Permit and exports from other countries require a Certificate of Origin.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. It describes the rules of Appendix II, not Appendix I. Under Article II(2)(b) and Article IV of CITES, 'look-alike' species (listed so that trade in threatened species can be brought under effective control) and species that may become threatened unless trade is strictly regulated are placed in Appendix II. Trade in Appendix II specimens requires an Export Permit (or Re-export Certificate) based on a Non-Detriment Finding, whereas an Import Permit is not required by CITES unless mandated by stricter domestic law.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. It describes the rules of Appendix I, not Appendix II. Under Article II(1) and Article III of CITES, Appendix I lists species threatened with extinction which are or may be affected by trade. Trade in specimens of these species is permitted only in exceptional, non-commercial circumstances and requires the prior grant and presentation of both an Import Permit (confirming the specimen is not to be used for primarily commercial purposes) and an Export Permit.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Under Article II(3) and Article V of CITES, Appendix III contains species identified by any Party as being subject to regulation within its jurisdiction for the purpose of preventing or restricting exploitation, and as needing the cooperation of other Parties in the control of trade. Unlike Appendices I and II (which require a two-thirds majority vote of the CoP to amend), a Party can unilaterally list a native species in Appendix III. Export from the State that included the species in Appendix III requires an Export Permit, while export from any other State requires a Certificate of Origin.

ref: CITES Text Articles II, III, IV & V

stem: With reference to the domestic implementation of CITES in India under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 (as amended by the Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The 2022 Amendment inserted a dedicated Chapter VB into the Act to regulate international trade in endangered species and placed CITES-listed specimens under Schedule IV of the Act.

2. Under the amended Act, the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) is designated as India's statutory CITES Management Authority, while the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) serves as the CITES Scientific Authority.

3. Every person possessing a living specimen of a scheduled species listed in Schedule IV is legally mandated to report the details of such specimen and obtain a registration certificate from the Management Authority.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 rationalized the Act's schedules from six to four—placing CITES-listed specimens in Schedule IV—and inserted Chapter VB (Sections 49D–49R) to give full statutory backing to CITES in India. It empowers the Central Government to designate an officer not below the rank of Additional Director General of Forests as the Management Authority and specialized research institutes as Scientific Authorities.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 abolished the older six-schedule framework and replaced it with four Schedules: Schedule I (animal species with highest protection), Schedule II (animal species with lesser protection), Schedule III (protected plant species), and Schedule IV (specimens listed in the Appendices under CITES). It also inserted Chapter VB ('Regulation of International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora as per CITES').

Statement 2 is incorrect. Under Section 49E of the amended Wildlife (Protection) Act, the Central Government appoints an officer not below the rank of an Additional Director General of Forests as the CITES Management Authority (the Director of Wildlife Preservation, MoEFCC), not the National Biodiversity Authority. Furthermore, under Section 49F, the Central Government designates premier research institutes (such as the Zoological Survey of India, Botanical Survey of India, Wildlife Institute of India, CMFRI, and ICFRE) as Scientific Authorities—whereas the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) is an enforcement agency that assists in curbing illegal wildlife trade, not a Scientific Authority.

Statement 3 is correct. Under Section 49M of the Wildlife (Protection) Act (operationalized through the Living Animal Species (Reporting and Registration) Rules, 2024), any person in possession of a living specimen of a species listed in Schedule IV must report the details of such specimen and apply electronically (via the PARIVESH 2.0 portal) for registration with the Management Authority, as well as report any subsequent transfer, birth of offspring, or death.

ref: Wildlife (Protection) Amendment Act, 2022 (Chapter VB, Sections 49D-49R & Schedule IV); Living Animal Species (Reporting and Registration) Rules, 2024

stem: With reference to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Under Article VII of CITES, specimens of an animal species listed in Appendix I that are bred in captivity for commercial purposes at CITES-registered facilities are legally treated as if they are specimens of species included in Appendix II.

Statement-II: The CITES Secretariat is jointly administered and financed by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) through the TRAFFIC network.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Article VII(4) of CITES creates a regulated legal fiction whereby captive-bred Appendix I animals from Secretariat-registered operations (and artificially propagated Appendix I plants) are traded under Appendix II rules to incentivize ex-situ breeding over wild harvesting. Institutionally, the CITES Secretariat is administered by UNEP rather than IUCN or WWF.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. While international trade in wild-caught specimens of Appendix I species for primarily commercial purposes is strictly prohibited under Article III of CITES, Article VII(4) provides a critical statutory exemption: specimens of an animal species included in Appendix I bred in captivity for commercial purposes (at breeding operations registered with the CITES Secretariat), or of a plant species included in Appendix I artificially propagated for commercial purposes, are legally deemed to be specimens of species included in Appendix II and can be traded with export permits.

Statement-II is incorrect. Although CITES originated from a 1963 resolution of the IUCN and relies on scientific technical support from IUCN and trade monitoring by TRAFFIC (which is a joint programme of WWF and IUCN), the CITES Secretariat itself is administered by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in Geneva and is financed through the CITES Trust Fund via contributions from Party States.

ref: CITES Text Articles III, VII(4) & XII; UNEP-CITES Institutional Framework

stem: With reference to the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), also known as the Bonn Convention, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Convention, a migratory species can be listed in both Appendix I and Appendix II simultaneously if conservation circumstances so warrant.
2. A State whose flag vessels are engaged outside national jurisdictional limits in taking a migratory species qualifies as a 'Range State' in relation to that species.
3. The Convention applies both to transboundary migratory wild fauna and to threatened coastal flora whose seeds or propagules disperse across international maritime boundaries.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Unlike CITES where Appendix I and Appendix II listings for the same population are mutually exclusive, Article IV(2) of the Bonn Convention explicitly allows a migratory animal species to be listed in both Appendix I and Appendix II simultaneously. Furthermore, CMS applies strictly to wild animals (fauna) and never to flora.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Article IV(2) of the Bonn Convention, if the circumstances so warrant, a migratory species may be listed both in Appendix I (requiring strict domestic protection against 'taking' by Range States) and in Appendix II (requiring Range States to conclude global or regional multilateral Agreements for its collaborative management).

Statement 2 is correct. Under Article I(1)(h) of CMS, a 'Range State' in relation to a particular migratory species means any State that exercises jurisdiction over any part of the land or water range which that species inhabits, stays in temporarily, or crosses, OR a State whose flag vessels are engaged outside national jurisdictional limits (such as on the high seas) in taking that migratory species.

Statement 3 is incorrect. As its formal title specifies, the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) applies exclusively to wild fauna (terrestrial, aquatic, and avian animals whose entire population or any geographically separate part cyclically and predictably crosses one or more national jurisdictional boundaries). It does not cover plants or flora.

ref: Bonn Convention (CMS) Articles I, III & IV

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the species-specific 'Agreements' and 'Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs)' concluded under the auspices of the Bonn Convention (CMS):
items: 1. A Range State can become a signatory or party to a specific Agreement or MoU concluded under CMS even if that State is not a Party to the parent Bonn Convention itself.
2. While Agreements concluded under Article IV of CMS are legally binding treaties, CMS Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) are legally non-binding instruments aimed at rapid conservation coordination.
3. India is a signatory to the CMS Memoranda of Understanding on the conservation of Siberian Cranes, Marine Turtles of the Indian Ocean and South-East Asia, Dugongs, and Raptors.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: To ensure ecologically seamless flyway and swimway conservation without diplomatic bottlenecks, Article V(2) of the Bonn Convention allows non-Party Range States to join specific daughter Agreements and MoUs under CMS without ratifying the parent Convention itself.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Because protecting a migratory species is biologically futile if key transit countries along its flyway or migratory corridor are excluded, Article V(2) of the Bonn Convention stipulates that every daughter Agreement or MoU concluded under CMS is open to accession or signature by all Range States of that migratory species, regardless of whether they are Parties to the parent CMS Convention.

Statement 2 is correct. CMS operates as a framework convention through two distinct classes of daughter instruments under Article IV: formal 'Agreements' (which are legally binding multilateral treaties requiring formal ratification) and less formal 'Memoranda of Understanding' (MoUs), which are legally non-binding administrative instruments designed for swift implementation by relevant ministries across Range States.

Statement 3 is correct. India (a Party to CMS since 1983) has signed four major non-binding CMS MoUs: the MoU on the Conservation of Siberian Cranes (1998), the Indian Ocean–South-East Asian (IOSEA) Marine Turtle MoU (2007), the MoU on the Conservation and Management of Dugongs and their Habitats (2008), and the MoU on the Conservation of Migratory Birds of Prey in Africa and Eurasia / Raptors MoU (2016).

ref: Bonn Convention Articles IV & V; MoEFCC CMS COP-13/COP-14 National Reports

stem: With reference to the functional differences between CITES and the Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS), consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Listing an endangered animal species in Appendix I of CITES does not directly obligate a Party State under international treaty law to protect the species' natural habitat or remove physical obstacles to its domestic movement, whereas listing it in Appendix I of CMS directly creates such in-situ obligations for Range States.

Statement-II: The regulatory jurisdiction of CITES is triggered strictly when a listed specimen or its derivative crosses an international border or is introduced from the high seas, whereas CMS regulates domestic 'taking', habitat restoration, and migratory connectivity across a species' biological range even when no international trade is involved.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: CITES and CMS address fundamentally different ecological threat vectors: CITES is a customs-border trade treaty triggered solely by cross-border movement or introduction from the sea, whereas CMS is an in-situ biological range treaty that mandates habitat conservation, obstacle removal, and domestic harvesting bans.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. CITES contains no binding provisions requiring Party States to protect domestic habitats, mitigate linear infrastructure barriers, or prevent domestic poaching if the specimen never enters international trade. By contrast, Article III(4) and III(5) of CMS explicitly obligate Range States of Appendix I species to conserve and restore important habitats, prevent or remove physical obstacles that seriously impede migration, and prohibit the domestic 'taking' (hunting, capturing, or harassing) of those animals.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. The reason CITES does not create in-situ habitat or migratory corridor obligations is that its legal trigger under Article I(c) is confined to 'trade'—defined strictly as export, re-export, import, and introduction from the sea of live or dead specimens and their readily recognizable parts and derivatives. Conversely, CMS is triggered by the biological migration of live populations across range jurisdictions, requiring comprehensive in-situ protection within each Range State's territory.

ref: CITES Articles I & III vs. Bonn Convention (CMS) Article III(4)-(5)

stem: With reference to the legal architecture and jurisdictional scope of the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, which one of the following statements is correct?

opts.A: The Convention imposes a blanket global prohibition on the transboundary movement of all Annex I hazardous wastes between all Party States, permitting international transport only for household municipal wastes.
opts.B: Radioactive wastes that are subject to other international control systems and wastes derived from the normal operations of a ship whose discharge is covered by another international instrument are explicitly excluded from the scope of the Convention.
opts.C: Once a consignment of hazardous waste has physically entered an Importing State through illegal traffic caused solely by the exporter, the legal and financial responsibility for its disposal shifts permanently to the Importing State.
opts.D: A Party to the Convention is legally permitted to export hazardous waste to a non-Party without any bilateral or regional intergovernmental agreement, provided written consent is obtained directly from the private recycling facility in the importing country.

core: To avoid overlapping treaty jurisdictions, Article 1(3) and Article 1(4) of the Basel Convention explicitly carve out two major waste streams from its scope: radioactive wastes governed by IAEA control systems, and wastes generated by the normal operations of ships governed by the IMO's MARPOL Convention.

exp.why: Option B is correct because under Article 1(3) and Article 1(4) of the Basel Convention, wastes which, as a result of being radioactive, are subject to other international control systems (such as IAEA instruments), and wastes which derive from the normal operations of a ship, the discharge of which is covered by another international instrument (such as MARPOL 73/78), are expressly excluded from the scope of the Basel Convention (though ship dismantling/breaking itself remains covered). Option A is incorrect because the parent Basel Convention regulates transboundary movement through the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure rather than a total global prohibition between all Parties. Option C is incorrect because under Article 9(2), when illegal traffic is the result of conduct on the part of the exporter or generator, the State of export is legally obligated to ensure that the wastes are taken back (re-imported) by the exporter, the generator, or the State of export itself within 30 days. Option D is incorrect because Article 4(5) strictly prohibits Parties from exporting hazardous wastes to, or importing them from, a non-Party unless the countries have entered into a formal bilateral, multilateral, or regional agreement under Article 11 that mandates environmentally sound management.

ref: Basel Convention Articles 1(3), 1(4), 4(5), 6 & 9

stem: With reference to the major amendments adopted under the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Basel Ban Amendment, member states of the OECD and the European Union (Annex VII countries) are prohibited from exporting hazardous wastes to non-Annex VII countries for final disposal, but are expressly permitted to export such hazardous wastes if destined strictly for recycling or resource recovery.

2. Following the Basel E-Waste Amendments (effective from 2025), even non-hazardous electrical and electronic waste is placed under Annex II and requires Prior Informed Consent (PIC) before any transboundary movement.

3. Under the Basel Plastic Waste Amendments, clean, uncontaminated single-polymer non-halogenated plastic waste destined exclusively for environmentally sound recycling remains in Annex IX and can be traded internationally without invoking the PIC procedure.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Basel Ban Amendment prohibits Annex VII (OECD/EU/Liechtenstein) Parties from exporting hazardous wastes to non-Annex VII developing countries for BOTH final disposal and recycling/recovery. Meanwhile, the 2025 E-Waste Amendments brought all non-hazardous e-waste under Annex II (requiring PIC), closing the repair/recycling loophole.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. The Basel Ban Amendment (Article 4A, which entered into force in December 2019) was specifically enacted to close the 'recycling loophole' through which toxic waste was dumped in developing nations under the guise of recycling. Article 4A(1) and 4A(2) legally obligate Parties listed in Annex VII (OECD members, the European Union, and Liechtenstein) to prohibit ALL transboundary movements of hazardous wastes to non-Annex VII States, both for final disposal operations AND for recovery, recycling, reclamation, direct re-use, or alternative uses.

Statement 2 is correct. Under the Basel E-Waste Amendments (adopted at COP-15 in 2022 and effective from 1 January 2025), the former Annex IX exemption (B1110) for non-hazardous e-waste was deleted. Hazardous e-waste is listed under entry A1181 in Annex VIII, while all other non-hazardous electrical and electronic waste, components, and scraps are placed under entry Y49 in Annex II ('Categories of wastes requiring special consideration'), thereby making all transboundary shipments of both hazardous and non-hazardous e-waste subject to mandatory Prior Informed Consent (PIC).

Statement 3 is correct. Under the Basel Plastic Waste Amendments (effective since 2021), hazardous plastic wastes (Annex VIII, A3210) and mixed, contaminated, or hard-to-recycle plastic wastes (Annex II, Y48) are subject to the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) regime. However, clean, sorted, uncontaminated single-polymer non-halogenated plastic waste (such as PE, PP, or PET) destined directly for recycling in an environmentally sound manner is listed under entry B3011 in Annex IX and remains exempt from the PIC requirement.

ref: Basel Convention Article 4A (Ban Amendment), COP-14 Plastic Amendments & COP-15 E-Waste Amendments (effective Jan 2025)

stem: With reference to the international regulation of transboundary movement of wastes and India's domestic legal framework, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While India is a Party to the Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes and Their Disposal, it has not ratified the Basel Ban Amendment.

2. Under the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the import of hazardous waste from any country into India for final disposal is completely prohibited.

3. Under the Basel Convention Plastic Waste Amendments, transboundary movement of mixed or contaminated plastic wastes is subject to the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure, whereas presorted and uncontaminated single-polymer recyclable plastic wastes are exempted from it.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: India balances its status as a Basel Convention Party with its domestic resource-recovery needs by refraining from ratifying the Basel Ban Amendment (which restricts secondary raw material imports for recycling from OECD countries), while strictly banning all hazardous waste imports meant for final disposal under its 2016 domestic Rules.

exp.why: India ratified the Basel Convention in 1992, but it has not ratified the 1995 Basel Ban Amendment (which entered into force globally in December 2019). The Ban Amendment prohibits all exports of hazardous wastes—even for recycling and recovery—from Annex VII countries (OECD, EU, and Liechtenstein) to non-Annex VII countries.

Under Rule 12(1) of the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 (notified under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986), no import of hazardous and other wastes from any country to India is permitted for disposal. Import is permitted only for recycling, recovery, reuse, and utilization including co-processing.

The Basel Plastic Waste Amendments (effective January 2021) created three updated entries: Annex VIII (A3210, hazardous plastic waste) and Annex II (Y48, mixed or contaminated plastic waste requiring special consideration), both of which trigger the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure, while Annex IX (B3011) exempts clean, presorted, uncontaminated single-polymer plastics destined for environmentally sound recycling from the PIC requirement.

ref: Basel Convention Texts; Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 (MoEFCC)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade:
items: Statement-I: Once an industrial chemical or severely hazardous pesticide formulation is listed in Annex III of the Rotterdam Convention, all State Parties are legally bound to phase out its domestic production and international trade within ten years.

Statement-II: The Rotterdam Convention establishes a legally binding Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure under which importing Parties formally decide whether to accept or refuse future shipments of Annex III chemicals, and exporting Parties must ensure that exporters within their jurisdiction comply with those decisions.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Unlike the Stockholm Convention (which mandates the elimination or restriction of listed POPs), listing a chemical in Annex III of the Rotterdam Convention does not constitute a global ban or phase-out; it triggers mandatory information exchange and the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) trade mechanism.

exp.why: This statement confuses the Rotterdam Convention with the Stockholm Convention. Listing a chemical or pesticide (such as Iprodione, Terbufos, or Paraquat formulations) in Annex III of the Rotterdam Convention does not ban or mandate a phase-out of its domestic production, use, or international trade.

Under Articles 10 and 11 of the Rotterdam Convention, for every chemical listed in Annex III, a Decision Guidance Document (DGD) is circulated to all Parties. Importing Parties must transmit an import response (consent, no consent, or consent subject to conditions), and exporting Parties are legally obligated to ensure that exporters under their jurisdiction respect those import responses.

ref: Rotterdam Convention Articles 10 & 11; UNEP BRS Conventions Compendium

stem: With reference to the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Persistent Organic Pollutants regulated under the Convention are characterized by high water solubility (hydrophilicity) and low lipid solubility, which enables them to dissolve rapidly in cellular fluids and biomagnify across aquatic food chains.

2. While chemicals listed in Annex A of the Convention are targeted for elimination, Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) is placed in Annex B to restrict its production and use to acceptable purposes such as disease vector control in accordance with World Health Organization guidelines.

3. Polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/PCDF) are listed in Annex C of the Convention, which regulates chemicals formed and released unintentionally from anthropogenic thermal and industrial processes.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) biomagnify across trophic levels precisely because they are hydrophobic (low water solubility) and lipophilic (fat-soluble), causing them to partition into and accumulate within the adipose tissues of organisms rather than being excreted via aqueous pathways.

exp.why: POPs are characterized by low water solubility (hydrophobicity) and high lipid/fat solubility (lipophilicity), alongside resistance to environmental degradation and semi-volatility (enabling long-range atmospheric transport). If a pollutant were highly water-soluble, organisms would readily excrete it in urine or across gills; because POPs are lipophilic, they bioaccumulate in fatty (adipose) tissues and biomagnify up the food chain.

Annex A lists chemicals slated for elimination (such as Aldrin, Chlordane, and Hexachlorobenzene), whereas Annex B lists chemicals subject to restriction. DDT (along with Perfluorooctane sulfonic acid - PFOS) is listed in Annex B, allowing registered Parties to produce and use DDT specifically for disease vector control (such as malaria) in accordance with WHO recommendations when locally safe, effective, and affordable alternatives are unavailable.

Annex C of the Stockholm Convention covers the unintentional production and release of POPs—specifically polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/PCDF), hexachlorobenzene (HCB), pentachlorobenzene (PeCB), polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), and polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs)—requiring Parties to apply Best Available Techniques (BAT) and Best Environmental Practices (BEP) to minimize and ultimately eliminate their release.

ref: Stockholm Convention Text (Annexes A, B, C & D); UNEP POPs Guidelines

stem: With reference to the legal procedure for adding new chemicals to the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) and its implementation in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Whenever the Conference of the Parties (COP) amends Annex A, B, or C to list a new chemical, the amendment automatically enters into force for all State Parties without exception upon the expiry of one year from its communication by the Depositary.

2. By virtue of India's declaration under Article 25(4) of the Convention, newly listed chemicals in Annexes A, B, or C—such as Methoxychlor, Dechlorane Plus, and UV-328—become legally binding on India only after India deposits a specific instrument of ratification or acceptance for those amendments.

3. In India, domestic rules prohibiting the manufacture, trade, use, import, and export of ratified Persistent Organic Pollutants are notified by the Central Government under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Article 25(4) of the Stockholm Convention, States that make an 'opt-in' declaration at the time of ratification (including India) are not automatically bound by subsequent COP amendments adding new POPs to Annexes A, B, or C unless they specifically deposit an instrument of ratification or acceptance for each new amendment.

exp.why: Under Articles 22(3)-(4) and 25(4) of the Stockholm Convention, amendments to Annex A, B, or C do not automatically bind all Parties without exception. First, under the standard 'opt-out' procedure (Article 22(3)(b)), any Party may notify the depositary within one year that it is unable to accept an amendment. Second, under Article 25(4), a Party may declare upon ratification that any amendment to Annex A, B, or C shall enter into force for it only upon the deposit of its instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval, or accession with respect to that amendment ('opt-in' track).

When India ratified the Stockholm Convention in January 2006, it opted for the Article 25(4) declaration regime. Consequently, newly added POPs (such as the initial 9 new POPs or recently listed ones like Methoxychlor, Dechlorane Plus, and UV-328) do not bind India automatically after one year; the Union Cabinet must approve and deposit a specific instrument of ratification for those chemicals.

To give domestic legal effect to the ratification of POPs under the Stockholm Convention, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) notifies the Regulation of Persistent Organic Pollutants Rules in exercise of powers conferred by Sections 3 and 6 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

ref: Stockholm Convention Articles 22 & 25(4); MoEFCC Regulation of Persistent Organic Pollutants Rules under EPA 1986

stem: With reference to the Minamata Convention on Mercury, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Convention imposes an immediate, non-derogable global prohibition on all use of elemental mercury in Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM) as well as on the clinical use of mercury-containing dental amalgam.

2. Under Annex A of the Convention, vaccines containing thiomersal (an ethylmercury compound used as a preservative) are subject to mandatory phase-out on the same timeline as mercury-added switches, relays, and cosmetics.

3. The scope of the Convention is confined strictly to the mining of primary mercury and trade in mercury-added consumer products, and therefore excludes atmospheric point-source mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants and cement clinker production facilities.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Minamata Convention regulates the entire anthropogenic lifecycle of mercury—from primary mining and product phase-outs to industrial point-source emissions (coal plants, cement, non-ferrous smelting)—while adopting pragmatic phase-down/National Action Plan frameworks for Artisanal Gold Mining (ASGM) and dental amalgam, and exempting thiomersal-preserved vaccines.

exp.why: Under Article 7 and Annex C, the Minamata Convention does not impose a blanket ban on mercury use in Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM); instead, Parties with more than insignificant ASGM must develop and implement a National Action Plan (NAP) to reduce, and where feasible eliminate, mercury use while prohibiting specific worst practices (such as whole ore amalgamation and open burning of amalgam without vapor traps). Similarly, under Annex A Part II, dental amalgam is placed under a 'phase-down' framework rather than an immediate absolute ban.

Annex A of the Minamata Convention explicitly excludes vaccines containing thiomersal as preservatives from the list of mercury-added products subject to phase-out (alongside products essential for civil protection and military uses, and products for research and instrument calibration where no mercury-free alternative is available).

Under Article 8 and Annex D, the Minamata Convention explicitly regulates atmospheric mercury emissions from five major industrial point-source categories: coal-fired power plants, coal-fired industrial boilers, smelting and roasting processes used in the production of non-ferrous metals, waste incineration facilities, and cement clinker production facilities.

ref: Minamata Convention Text (Articles 4, 7, 8 & Annexes A, C, D); UNEP Mercury Assessment

stem: Consider the following pairs of multilateral environmental regulatory instruments/mechanisms and the respective international conventions under which they operate:
items: 1. Circulation of Decision Guidance Documents (DGDs) to assist national import decisions : Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants
2. Prohibition on hazardous exports from Annex VII (OECD/EU) to Non-Annex VII countries : Basel Convention on Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes
3. Mandatory Best Available Techniques to minimize unintentional releases listed in Annex C : Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants
4. Mandatory National Action Plans for Artisanal and Small-Scale Gold Mining (ASGM) : Minamata Convention on Mercury
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: While the Basel, Rotterdam, and Stockholm (BRS) Conventions share a common Secretariat and utilize the Global Environment Facility (GEF) alongside the Minamata Convention, each treaty employs distinct technical mechanisms: Rotterdam circulates Decision Guidance Documents (DGDs) via its Chemical Review Committee, whereas Stockholm prepares Risk Profiles and Risk Management Evaluations via the POPs Review Committee.

exp.why: Decision Guidance Documents (DGDs) are drafted by the Chemical Review Committee (CRC) and circulated under Article 7 of the Rotterdam Convention (not the Stockholm Convention) for every chemical listed in Annex III to assist importing Parties in making informed decisions under the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure. Under the Stockholm Convention, the POPs Review Committee (POPRC) prepares a Risk Profile (Annex E) and a Risk Management Evaluation (Annex F).

Under the Basel Ban Amendment (Article 4A and Annex VII of the Basel Convention), Parties listed in Annex VII (members of the OECD, the European Union, and Liechtenstein) are prohibited from exporting hazardous wastes intended for final disposal, recovery, or recycling to countries not listed in Annex VII.

Article 5 and Annex C of the Stockholm Convention require Parties to apply Best Available Techniques (BAT) and promote Best Environmental Practices (BEP) to continuously minimize and, where feasible, eliminate releases of unintentionally produced POPs (such as dioxins, furans, PCBs, and HCB).

Under Article 7 and Annex C of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, any Party that notifies the Secretariat that artisanal and small-scale gold mining and processing within its territory is more than insignificant is legally obligated to develop and implement a National Action Plan (NAP) and review progress every three years.

ref: BRS Conventions Synergies Manual (UNEP); Minamata Convention Article 7

stem: With reference to the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer and its Kigali Amendment, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Although Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) have zero Ozone Depleting Potential (ODP), they were brought under the regulatory ambit of the Montreal Protocol because their industrial proliferation occurred directly as chemical substitutes for CFCs and HCFCs phased out under the Protocol.
2. Under the Kigali Amendment, India is classified in Group 1 of Article 5 Parties and is mandated to freeze its HFC production and consumption in 2024 and achieve an 80% reduction by 2045.

3. Unlike the Kyoto Protocol which grouped greenhouse gases into a single emissions basket, the Kigali Amendment mandates a structured phase-down of the actual production and consumption of controlled HFCs measured in carbon dioxide equivalents, supported financially by the Multilateral Fund of the Montreal Protocol.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) lack chlorine or bromine atoms and therefore have zero Ozone Depleting Potential (ODP), but possess extremely high Global Warming Potential (GWP); they are regulated under the Montreal Protocol via the Kigali Amendment because the refrigeration and air-conditioning sectors adopted them as direct replacements for ozone-depleting CFCs and HCFCs. Under the Kigali Amendment, India belongs to Group 2 of Article 5 (developing) Parties, with a baseline of 2024–2026, a freeze year of 2028, and an 85% reduction target by 2047.

exp.why: HFCs are synthetic fluorinated compounds containing hydrogen, fluorine, and carbon, but no chlorine or bromine; hence they do not catalytically destroy stratospheric ozone (ODP = 0). However, because the Montreal Protocol's sector-by-sector phase-out of CFCs and HCFCs drove the global transition toward HFCs, Parties used the Montreal Protocol's proven industrial compliance machinery via the 2016 Kigali Amendment (adding Annex F substances) to phase down high-GWP HFCs.

The Kigali Amendment divides Article 5 (developing) Parties into two groups. Most developing nations fall in Group 1 (baseline 2020–2022, freeze in 2024, and 80% reduction by 2045). However, India—along with Gulf states, Iran, Iraq, and Pakistan—secured placement in Group 2 of Article 5 Parties due to high ambient temperatures and growing cooling needs, giving India a baseline of 2024–2026, a freeze year of 2028, a 10% cut by 2032, and an 85% reduction by 2047.

While the UNFCCC/Kyoto architecture regulated HFCs as part of a multi-gas emissions basket, the Kigali Amendment regulates the upstream industrial supply side—phasing down the actual production and consumption of Annex F HFCs weighted by their 100-year GWP in CO2 equivalents—and utilizes the Montreal Protocol's Multilateral Fund to finance technology conversion in Article 5 countries.

ref: Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol (2016); MoEFCC India Cooling Action Plan & Ozone Cell Notifications

stem: With reference to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under Article 1 of the Convention, 'desertification' is legally defined as the physical outward expansion of natural hyper-arid deserts into adjacent fertile biomes driven by climate change.
2. The Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) Target-Setting Programme under the UNCCD assigns uniform, legally binding quantitative restoration quotas to all Parties through a mandatory compliance Annex.

3. The Permanent Secretariat of the UNCCD is administratively governed by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) in Nairobi, and its core implementation is financed through the Adaptation Fund.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Article 1 of the UNCCD, desertification does not refer to the physical expansion of existing hyper-arid deserts, but specifically to land degradation in arid, semi-arid, and dry sub-humid areas (where the aridity index ranges between 0.05 and 0.65, excluding hyper-arid zones). While the UNCCD itself is a legally binding treaty implemented via Regional Implementation Annexes and National Action Programmes, its Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) Target-Setting Programme operates through voluntary national targets aligned with SDG 15.3.

exp.why: Under Article 1(a) and 1(g) of the UNCCD, 'desertification' is defined as 'land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from various factors, including climatic variations and human activities.' The Convention explicitly defines affected drylands as areas (other than polar and sub-polar regions) in which the ratio of annual precipitation to potential evapotranspiration falls within the range from 0.05 to 0.65, thereby excluding hyper-arid deserts (<0.05) and focusing on soil productivity loss rather than literal desert boundary movement.

Although the UNCCD is the sole legally binding international agreement linking environment and development to sustainable land management, the Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) Target-Setting Programme (operationalizing SDG Target 15.3 by 2030) invites countries to formulate voluntary national LDN targets tailored to national circumstances, rather than imposing uniform quantitative annex quotas.

The UNCCD Permanent Secretariat is headquartered in Bonn, Germany (not Nairobi) and is institutionally linked to the United Nations Secretariat rather than administered by UNEP. Moreover, the Global Environment Facility (GEF)—through its Land Degradation Focal Area—alongside the Global Mechanism (GM) of the UNCCD serves as the Convention's primary financial mechanism, rather than the Adaptation Fund (which serves the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement).

ref: UNCCD Text (Articles 1, 20, 21 & 23); UNCCD Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) Scientific Conceptual Framework

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the international legal governance of Marine Genetic Resources (MGRs):
items: Statement-I: The Nagoya Protocol to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) regulates the access and fair benefit-sharing of Marine Genetic Resources collected from both Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) and Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (the High Seas and the Area).

Statement-II: Under Article 4 of the Convention on Biological Diversity, with respect to components of biological diversity, the jurisdictional scope of the Convention is restricted to areas within the limits of national jurisdiction, whereas the BBNJ Agreement under UNCLOS governs the access and benefit-sharing of Marine Genetic Resources in Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Under Article 4(a) of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), with respect to the actual components of biological diversity (such as genetic resources), the treaty's jurisdictional scope applies only within the limits of national jurisdiction (such as territorial waters and EEZs). Consequently, the CBD and its Nagoya Protocol could not regulate Marine Genetic Resources (MGRs) in Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (ABNJ), a legal vacuum now filled by the 2023 BBNJ Agreement (High Seas Treaty) under UNCLOS.

exp.why: Under Article 3 of the Nagoya Protocol, its scope applies solely to genetic resources within the scope of Article 15 of the CBD—which is grounded in the sovereign rights of States over natural resources within their national jurisdiction (including internal waters, territorial seas, and EEZs). It has no jurisdiction over genetic resources harvested from the High Seas or the international seabed ('the Area').

Article 4(a) of the CBD limits the Convention's direct application over components of biological diversity to areas within national jurisdiction (while Article 4(b) covers only processes and activities carried out under a Party's jurisdiction or control beyond national jurisdiction). To address this gap, the Agreement under UNCLOS on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement) established a dedicated multilateral mechanism for benefit-sharing from MGRs and Digital Sequence Information (DSI) of ABNJ.

ref: Convention on Biological Diversity (Articles 4 & 15); Nagoya Protocol (Article 3); UNCLOS BBNJ Agreement (Part II)

stem: Consider the following pairs of Multilateral Environmental Agreements and their institutional governance architecture:
items: 1. Minamata Convention on Mercury : The Global Environment Facility (GEF) forms part of its designated financial mechanism, and its Secretariat is administered by UNEP.
2. Ramsar Convention on Wetlands : The Global Environment Facility (GEF) serves as its formally designated treaty financial mechanism, and its Secretariat is administered by UNEP.

3. Montreal Protocol on Ozone Depleting Substances : The Green Climate Fund (GCF) serves as its dedicated treaty financial mechanism, and its Secretariat is hosted by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
4. CITES (Washington Convention) : The Global Environment Facility (GEF) serves as its formally designated treaty financial mechanism, and its Secretariat is hosted by IUCN.
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Global Environment Facility (GEF) serves as a formally designated financial mechanism for six multilateral conventions: CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD, the Stockholm Convention on POPs, the Minamata Convention on Mercury, and the BBNJ Agreement. Treaties such as the Ramsar Convention (whose Secretariat is hosted by IUCN, outside the UN system) and CITES (administered by UNEP) are not formal GEF conventions, while the Montreal Protocol operates its own standalone Multilateral Fund.

exp.why: Under Article 13 of the Minamata Convention on Mercury, its financial mechanism comprises the Global Environment Facility (GEF) Trust Fund and a Specific International Programme to support capacity-building and technical assistance. Under Article 24, the Secretariat of the Minamata Convention is provided by the Executive Director of UNEP and is based in Geneva.

The Ramsar Convention (1971) is an intergovernmental treaty that operates outside the United Nations treaty system; its Secretariat is administratively hosted by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) in Gland, Switzerland, not by UNEP. Furthermore, the GEF is not a formally designated financial mechanism of the Ramsar Convention (wetland projects receive GEF funding only indirectly through the CBD Biodiversity or International Waters focal areas).

Under Article 10 of the Montreal Protocol, its dedicated financial mechanism is the Multilateral Fund for the Implementation of the Montreal Protocol (headquartered in Montreal), not the Green Climate Fund. Additionally, the Ozone Secretariat for the Vienna Convention and Montreal Protocol is administered by UNEP in Nairobi, not by the WMO.

Although CITES grew out of a 1963 IUCN resolution, Article XII of CITES entrusts the administration of its Secretariat to the Executive Director of UNEP (located in Geneva), not IUCN. Moreover, CITES is not one of the six conventions for which the GEF serves as an official financial mechanism; it is funded through the CITES Trust Fund and voluntary external contributions.

ref: GEF Instrument for the Establishment of the Restructured GEF; Minamata Convention Art. 13 & 24; CITES Art. XII; Ramsar Convention Institutional Framework

stem: In the institutional architecture of global environmental governance, three multilateral treaties are officially designated as the 'Rio Conventions' because they emerged directly from the 1992 United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (Earth Summit) and coordinate their synergistic implementation through a Joint Liaison Group (JLG) established in 2001. Which of the following correctly identifies these three Rio Conventions?

opts.A: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and a legally binding Rio Convention on Global Forests
opts.B: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, and the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES)
opts.C: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, and the Convention on Migratory Species (CMS)
opts.D: The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD)

core: The three 'Rio Conventions' stemming from the 1992 Rio Earth Summit (UNCED) are the UNFCCC (climate change), the CBD (biodiversity), and the UNCCD (desertification/land degradation). In 2001, their Secretariats established the Joint Liaison Group (JLG) to coordinate cross-cutting synergies across climate adaptation, ecosystem restoration, and biodiversity conservation.

exp.why: Option D is correct because the 1992 Rio Earth Summit opened two legally binding treaties for signature—the UNFCCC and the CBD—and directly mandated the negotiation of a third legally binding treaty in Agenda 21 (Chapter 12), which was adopted in 1994 as the UNCCD. Together, UNFCCC, CBD, and UNCCD form the three 'Rio Conventions' linked via the Joint Liaison Group (JLG). Option A is incorrect because negotiations for a legally binding global forest treaty collapsed at Rio due to North-South disagreements over timber sovereignty, resulting only in the non-legally binding 'Forest Principles'. Options B and C are incorrect because Ramsar (1971), CITES (1973), and CMS (1979) predated the 1992 Rio Summit, while the Stockholm Convention on POPs was adopted later in 2001.

ref: UNCED 1992 Outcome Documents; CBD-UNFCCC-UNCCD Joint Liaison Group Terms of Reference

stem: Under India's constitutional and legal framework, consider the following procedural stages through which a newly negotiated Multilateral Environmental Agreement (MEA) progresses from international adoption to enforceable domestic statutory obligations against private entities in India:
items: 1. Enactment of implementing legislation by Parliament under Article 253 of the Constitution (or notification of subordinate statutory rules under an existing parent Act such as the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986) to translate the ratified treaty's international obligations into enforceable municipal law.
2. Adoption of the final text of the Multilateral Environmental Agreement at a Diplomatic Conference of Plenipotentiaries and signature by India's authorized representative subject to ratification.
3. Approval of treaty ratification by the Union Cabinet in exercise of the Union Executive power under Article 73 read with Entry 14 of the Union List.
4. Deposit of the formal Instrument of Ratification by the Government of India with the designated Treaty Depositary, triggering the treaty's international entry into force for India.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the stages given above?
core: India follows a dualist constitutional framework regarding the domestic enforceability of international treaties that alter domestic law or impose obligations on citizens. While negotiating, signing, and ratifying a treaty are purely executive functions performed by the Union Cabinet under Article 73 (read with Entry 14 of List I) followed by depositing the Instrument of Ratification internationally, domestic legal enforcement requires either Parliamentary legislation under Article 253 or statutory rule-making under an existing parent Act.

exp.why: Stage 1 is the final step (fourth in sequence): because India follows the dualist doctrine for domestic enforcement of treaty obligations affecting private rights, penalties, or state-list subjects, international ratification alone does not make treaty provisions self-executing municipal law. Following ratification, Parliament enacts implementing legislation under Article 253 (such as the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 to operationalize the CBD, which India ratified in 1994) or the Executive notifies subordinate rules under an existing parent statute like the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (such as the Ozone Depleting Substances Rules, 2000 following India's accession to the Montreal Protocol).

Stage 2 is the first step in the sequence: the treaty text is adopted at an international Conference of Plenipotentiaries and signed by India's accredited representative. Under Article 18 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, signature (when subject to ratification) authenticates the text and obliges the state not to defeat the object and purpose of the treaty, but does not yet establish binding consent to be bound.

Stage 3 is the second step in the sequence: unlike the United States where Senate advice and consent is required prior to ratification, treaty ratification in India is an executive act under Article 73 read with Entry 14 of List I (Seventh Schedule), approved by the Union Cabinet and executed in the name of the President.

Stage 4 is the third step in the sequence: following Union Cabinet approval, the Ministry of External Affairs deposits the formal Instrument of Ratification (or Accession/Acceptance) with the designated Depositary (such as the UN Secretary-General), upon which the treaty enters into force for India under international law after the stipulated waiting period.

ref: Constitution of India (Articles 51(c), 73 & 253; Seventh Schedule List I Entry 14); Supreme Court in Jolly George Varghese v. Bank of Cochin & Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. UoI
